A.q: A 64-year-old man is admitted with an inferior myocardial infarction. His heart rate falls to 46 with narrow QRS complexes and P waves that are either inverted (retrograde P waves) or buried in the QRS. Which rhythm is most likely?
opts: Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, not inverted P waves at 46.
Focal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm above 100 from one atrial focus; his rhythm is slow at 46.
ruled out by a stated finding
Sinus bradycardia keeps an upright, normal P wave before each QRS; his are inverted or buried.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A regular narrow rhythm at 40 to 60 with inverted or buried P waves is a junctional rhythm, and inferior myocardial infarction is a listed cause.

A.q: An 84-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has fatigue and dizziness. Her electrocardiogram shows P waves and wide QRS complexes at two separate rates with no relationship, the ventricular rate 36. She has had no tick bites, infections or recent procedures. Which cause of this rhythm is most likely?
opts: Correct. Third-degree block is most commonly from acquired disease of the conduction system, especially degenerative changes of old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes; an elderly hypertensive patient without infection fits best.
Lyme carditis is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no tick bites; the most common cause in an elderly hypertensive patient is degenerative conduction disease.
ruled out by a stated finding
Increased vagal tone is a listed cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block in conditioned people; complete block in an 84-year-old is most often degenerative.
Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no infection; degenerative disease of old age is far more common.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure is admitted with pneumonia and a low oxygen level. His pulse is irregular at 120. His electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every narrow QRS, but the P waves take at least three different shapes in the same lead and the intervals between beats vary. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is also irregular but has no P waves at all on the tracing; this rhythm has a P wave before every QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An irregular, narrow-complex tachycardia with a P wave before each QRS in at least three shapes is multifocal atrial tachycardia, from multiple atrial foci, typically in acutely ill patients with lung disease or heart failure.
Focal atrial tachycardia comes from a single focus, so it is regular with one consistent abnormal P-wave shape; his P waves take three shapes.
Sinus arrhythmia has uniform P waves at 60 to 100 with a breathing-linked pattern; his rate is 120 with several P-wave shapes.

A.q: A 65-year-old man has a painful, swollen right groin two days after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. Ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall, communicating with the lumen. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes with palpable pulses. A post-catheterization cavity outside the arterial wall is a pseudoaneurysm.

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm is a communication between the arterial lumen and overlying connective tissue after arterial rupture; the common site is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, from laceration by the access needle.
Acute limb ischemia is a sudden occlusion with a cold, pale, pulseless limb. A painful groin swelling with an extraluminal cavity is a pseudoaneurysm.
A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall. A cavity outside the wall after needle laceration is a false aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm.

A.q: A 72-year-old man is diagnosed with an acute aortic dissection. His family asks what happens if it is not treated. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Correct. Acute untreated aortic dissection carries a high mortality rate, which is why blood pressure is lowered at once, pain is controlled and surgical grafting of the diseased aorta is pursued.
Only the legs are at risk
Dissection is an intimal tear of the aorta itself, with syncope, blood pressure swings and aortic regurgitation. Untreated, mortality is high.
Nothing supports spontaneous healing as the expected course. Acute untreated dissection has a high mortality rate.
A pseudoaneurysm is a separate lesion from arterial puncture. The danger of untreated acute dissection is a high mortality rate.

A.q: A 68-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure is told her palpitations come from atrial flutter. She is stable. Which description best fits her electrocardiogram?
opts: Sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes
Correct. In atrial flutter, sawtooth (flutter) waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more outnumber the narrow QRS complexes, most often conducted 2:1, so the ventricular rhythm is usually regular.
One abnormal P wave before every QRS
One abnormal P wave before each QRS is focal atrial tachycardia; in flutter there are more atrial waves than QRS complexes.
No P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm
Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm describe atrial fibrillation; flutter has organized sawtooth waves and is usually regular.
Three or more P-wave shapes in one lead
At least three P-wave shapes in one lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia; flutter waves are identical to one another, in a sawtooth line.

A.q: A 41-year-old woman has had palpitations for a month. The monitor reads a regular rate of 130, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which of the following would most likely account for this rhythm?
opts: Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, slowing the rate below 60; this sinus rhythm is fast, which points the other way.
Increased intracranial pressure appears among the causes of sinus bradycardia, not tachycardia; a fast sinus rhythm comes from pain, anxiety, hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia or hyperthyroidism.
Digoxin is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, along with beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; it slows the sinus rate rather than speeding it.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 130 with an upright P wave before every QRS is sinus tachycardia, which usually reflects a physiologic or pathologic process; hyperthyroidism is one of the listed pathologic causes.
A.alt: Rhythm strip with closely spaced, regular narrow complexes, each preceded by an upright P wave

A.q: An 80-year-old man is found unresponsive and pulseless. The monitor shows a flat line in two leads with no P waves or QRS complexes. Compressions are underway. Which drug is a mainstay of treatment?
opts: Lidocaine is considered in shock-refractory fibrillation. Asystole is treated with compressions and epinephrine.
Correct. High-quality chest compressions and epinephrine by intravenous or intraosseous push at intervals are the mainstays of treatment for asystole.
Amiodarone is for shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia. Asystole relies on compressions and epinephrine.
Magnesium treats torsades de pointes. Asystole is treated with compressions and epinephrine.

A.q: A 56-year-old woman has fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin and a heart rate of 54. Echocardiogram shows a large pericardial effusion without chamber collapse. Which test best addresses the cause her features suggest?
opts: Tuberculosis is a cause where it is prevalent, but her features point to myxedema. Thyroid tests fit.
Correct. Hypothyroidism (myxedema) is a metabolic cause of pericardial effusion, and thyroid function tests are part of the effusion workup; her symptoms point straight at it.
An antinuclear antibody screens for lupus; her cold intolerance, weight gain and bradycardia point to hypothyroidism.
Cultures look for bacterial infection. Her picture suggests hypothyroidism, tested with thyroid function tests.

A.q: A 63-year-old man has an incidental 4.0 cm ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm on a chest radiograph and follow-up imaging. He has no symptoms. Which surveillance plan is appropriate?
opts: Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 3 to 5 years
Correct. Thoracic aneurysms under 4.5 cm are followed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every three to five years; 4.5 to 5.4 cm moves to every six to 12 months.
Abdominal ultrasound every three years with no other imaging
Three-yearly ultrasound is the plan for small abdominal aneurysms and cannot see the thoracic aorta. His surveillance is computed tomography or magnetic resonance.
Open repair with aortic root replacement within the month
Asymptomatic ascending repair is generally indicated above 5.5 cm or with growth over 0.5 cm per year. At 4.0 cm he needs surveillance, not surgery.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 6 to 12 months
Six-to-12-monthly imaging applies to thoracic aneurysms of 4.5 to 5.4 cm. At 4.0 cm the interval is every three to five years.

A.q: A 52-year-old man with uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis of the forearm after an intravenous catheter is discharged on warm compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug. He is anxious that the clot could travel to his lungs. Which follow-up instruction is most appropriate?
opts: Such a short interval is unnecessary for a stable outpatient with a low-risk superficial clot. The recheck to assess resolution or progression is set at 7 to 10 days.
Waiting 6 to 8 weeks would leave progression unrecognized for too long. The examination is due within 7 to 10 days to separate resolution from worsening.
Fever suggests infection within the vein, but progression of a clot can occur without it. A scheduled recheck within 7 to 10 days is needed, not follow-up only for fever.
Correct. A repeat examination within 7 to 10 days checks for resolution versus progression, and persistence or worsening prompts a repeat duplex ultrasound. He should return sooner if it worsens.

A.q: A 54-year-old man has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 210. His blood pressure is 72/40, and he is confused and sweating. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
opts: Adenosine is for the stable patient after a vagal maneuver; this patient is unstable and needs synchronized cardioversion.
A vagal maneuver is first line only for the stable patient; hypotension with confusion calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion.
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia (hypotension and confusion) gets immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage.
Defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; he has a pulse, so the shock must be synchronized.

A.q: A 77-year-old woman has no symptoms, but her routine electrocardiogram shows P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR interval and an occasional P wave not followed by a QRS. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observation suits asymptomatic first-degree or Mobitz type I block; Mobitz type II is dangerous even without symptoms and needs a permanent pacemaker.
Catheter ablation is itself a listed cause of Mobitz type II block and treats accessory pathways or reentry; this block needs a permanent pacemaker.

Correct. A constant PR with randomly dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz type II block, dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block and sudden death; the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Beta blockers are listed causes of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, not a treatment for block; Mobitz type II needs a permanent pacemaker.

A.q: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a car crash with a heart rate of 128 and a blood pressure of 88/56. The rhythm is regular with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Bedside ultrasound shows free fluid in the abdomen. Which is the most appropriate approach to her heart rate?
opts: Correct. This is appropriate sinus tachycardia from hypovolemia, a pathologic cause; management of appropriate sinus tachycardia is treating the underlying cause.
Adenosine is for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; a sinus tachycardia compensating for blood loss settles when the cause is treated.
Slowing a compensatory tachycardia in a hypovolemic patient would remove her compensation; the bleeding is what needs treatment.
Cardioversion cannot fix a compensatory sinus rhythm and would not restore her volume; the cause must be treated.

A.q: A 57-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis felt a sudden sharp pain behind the right knee while climbing stairs, followed by severe calf discomfort and swelling. Venous duplex ultrasound shows no thrombus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Superficial thrombophlebitis gives a tender, indurated cord along a superficial vein with local redness. A sudden severe calf pain that began behind the knee is not a superficial vein process.
A calf muscle tear follows an inciting injury and may leave bruising at the ankle. Here the pain began behind the knee during ordinary activity, which fits a ruptured cyst better.
Post-thrombotic syndrome is chronic venous insufficiency appearing 6 to 24 months after a clot, with slow-onset edema and skin change. A sudden calf event with no prior clot is not that.

Correct. A ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst produces severe, sudden calf discomfort that mimics deep vein thrombosis, and the ultrasound shows no clot. It is a standard item on the differential of a swollen calf.

A.q: A 36-year-old woman has bothersome palpitations from premature ventricular contractions. Her heart is structurally normal, she has never fainted, and her monitor shows a low burden of early beats. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: Reassurance and removing triggers suit low-risk patients with a low burden and no symptoms; her palpitations are bothersome, so a beta blocker is first line.
ruled out by a stated finding
An implantable defibrillator prevents sudden death after life-threatening ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation; low-risk premature beats do not need one.
Catheter ablation is for low-risk patients whose symptoms are refractory to, or who cannot tolerate, drug therapy; a beta blocker comes first.

Correct. In a low-risk patient with symptoms from premature ventricular contractions, a beta blocker is first line, with catheter ablation for symptoms that are refractory or a drug that cannot be tolerated.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: Constrictive pericarditis results from which change in the pericardium?
opts: Stiffening of the myocardium by infiltration
A stiff, infiltrated myocardium is restrictive cardiomyopathy, which sits in the differential of constriction. Constrictive pericarditis is scarring of the pericardium instead.
Acute inflammation lasting under six weeks
Inflammation lasting under 4 to 6 weeks is acute pericarditis. Constriction is the scarred, noncompliant pericardium that can follow repeated or chronic inflammation.
Rapid accumulation of fluid under pressure
Fluid accumulating under pressure and compressing the heart is cardiac tamponade. Constriction comes from a scarred, inelastic pericardium rather than from fluid.
Fibrous scarring with loss of elasticity
Correct. Constrictive pericarditis is fibrous scarring of the pericardium and loss of elasticity of the pericardial sac, producing pericardial noncompliance that limits filling.

A.q: Which device therapies are part of adult cardiomyopathy care?
opts: Correct. Adult device therapy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker, with an assist device or transplant considered in advanced cases.
Carotid stent or vena cava filter devices
These devices treat carotid stenosis and venous clot, not cardiomyopathy. Adult device therapy is a defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker.
External pacing is not the listed strategy. Adults receive an implantable defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker when indicated.
Intra-aortic balloon pump for all patients
A balloon pump is not listed as adult cardiomyopathy device therapy. The devices are a defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker.

A.q: A 31-year-old woman has sudden palpitations with visible pounding in her neck (frog sign). She is alert, with a blood pressure of 120/74. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Focal atrial tachycardia shows one abnormal P wave before every QRS; her P waves are hidden, and the neck pulsations of the frog sign point to nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with at least three P-wave shapes, usually in acutely ill lung patients; her rhythm is regular with no visible P waves.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; her tachycardia is regular, starts suddenly and comes with neck pulsations, which fits nodal reentry.

Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with hidden P waves and neck pulsations (frog sign) in a young woman is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, a reentry circuit within the node, far more common in women.

A.q: A 79-year-old woman has a week of fatigue and dizziness. Her heart rate is 36. The electrocardiogram shows regular P waves at 80 per minute and regular wide QRS complexes at 36 per minute, with no consistent relationship between them; some P waves sit inside T waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mobitz type II conducts most P waves at a constant PR and drops some. Here no P wave relates to any QRS.
Correct. Two separate regular rhythms, with atria faster than the ventricles and P waves falling anywhere (even within T waves), is third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block.
Mobitz type I shows a PR that lengthens until a drop. Here there is no consistent PR at all.
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast wide rhythm of 100 to 250 per minute. A wide rhythm at 36 with dissociated P waves is complete block.

A.q: A 63-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency has two days of warmth, tenderness and spreading blanching redness of the lower leg, with a low-grade fever. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Cellulitis is an infection of the deeper skin and soft tissue that surface ointment does not reach. Oral antibiotics such as cephalexin or clindamycin are recommended.
Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone and do not treat infection. Warmth, tenderness and fever describe cellulitis, which requires an oral antibiotic.
Correct. Cellulitis complicating venous insufficiency is treated with oral antibiotics, and cephalexin or clindamycin is recommended. Topical therapy is not adequate for the infection.
A topical corticosteroid treats stasis dermatitis, and spreading warm redness with fever indicates infection. Suppressing inflammation would not clear cellulitis, which needs oral antibiotics.

A.q: Which electrolyte is given as an intravenous push and then as an infusion to break torsades de pointes?
opts: Low potassium is a cause of a long QT and should be corrected, but the drug that breaks torsades is intravenous magnesium.
Phosphate plays no named role in torsades. Intravenous magnesium, then a magnesium infusion, is the treatment.
Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, and more magnesium is then given as an infusion; it is the main treatment.
Low calcium is a cause of a long QT, yet calcium is not the treatment that breaks torsades. Magnesium is.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive lung disease is admitted with an exacerbation. She is confused, and the monitor shows runs of skipped beats from frequent early, wide QRS complexes without P waves. Her arterial oxygen tension is low. Which underlying problem should be corrected first?
opts: Blood glucose is not a named trigger. Her low oxygen tension is the cause to correct first.
Temperature is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia, with electrolyte imbalance, drives premature ventricular contractions.
Correct. Hypoxemia is a main cause of premature ventricular contractions, along with electrolyte imbalance, so her low oxygen should be corrected first.
Blood pressure is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes of premature ventricular contractions.

A.q: A 70-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has pulmonary and systemic congestion, with crackles and leg edema. A diuretic is being started. Which statement about diuretic use in her is most accurate?
opts: Use with caution; stiff ventricles need preload

Correct. Diuretics are used for pulmonary and systemic congestion in restrictive cardiomyopathy, but with caution, because they lower preload and the noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output.
Only useful once the ejection fraction falls
Diuretics treat congestion whatever the ejection fraction, which is usually preserved until late. The caution is about lowering preload.
Give aggressively to fully dry the lungs
Aggressive diuresis drops the preload that stiff ventricles rely on and can collapse cardiac output. Diuretics are used, but cautiously.
Diuretics are not contraindicated; they treat the pulmonary and systemic congestion. They are simply used with caution because stiff ventricles need preload.

A.q: A 68-year-old woman has atrial fibrillation found at a routine visit. Her heart rate is 84, she has no symptoms of instability, and her blood pressure is 128/76. Which is the most appropriate rate management?
opts: Atropine speeds the heart and is used for unstable bradycardia; it has no role in rate-controlled atrial fibrillation.
Intravenous rate control is for rapid ventricular response; her rate of 84 is already controlled.
Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in atrial fibrillation without rapid ventricular response is managed with rate control by mouth, with anticoagulation guided by stroke risk.
Cardioversion is for instability or elective rhythm control after anticoagulation; she is stable.

A.q: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a stab wound to the left chest. He is hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, and a bedside scan shows blood in the pericardial space. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: A needle tap cannot stop ongoing bleeding from a cardiac wound; traumatic hemorrhagic tamponade needs surgery.
Diuretics lower preload and would worsen tamponade; the bleeding source must be repaired surgically.

Anti-inflammatories treat pericarditis, not a bleeding stab wound in the heart that needs repair.

Several months is the indolent pace of subacute disease. Untreated acute endocarditis progresses to death within weeks.
A years-long course would be closer to subacute, indolent disease. Untreated acute endocarditis kills within weeks.

Septal ablation treats outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Fluid retention in myocarditis is managed with a diuretic.
He is hemodynamically stable, so nothing calls for an inotrope. Fluid retention in myocarditis is treated with a diuretic as part of supportive care.
Thrombolytics dissolve clot and have no role in myocarditis fluid overload. A diuretic is added as needed for fluid retention.

Post-cardiac injury syndrome is grouped with idiopathic disease for the interleukin-1 blocker. Prednisone is reserved for systemic autoimmune disease.

Injection drug use in early childhood
Injection drug use becomes relevant only in adolescents. Young children's disease is driven by congenital heart disease and central lines.
Degenerative valve disease drives adult endocarditis in high-income countries, not pediatric disease.
Congenital heart disease has replaced rheumatic heart disease as the dominant pediatric substrate in developed countries.

Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, the polymorphic tachycardia of a prolonged QT; her QT was normal, which points to ischemia and calls for defibrillation.

Rheumatic carditis is an immune reaction to streptococci, not a complication of Candida endocarditis.
A pericardial knock belongs to constrictive pericarditis; fungal endocarditis embolizes to large arteries.
Fungal endocarditis is difficult to cure with medications alone and is an indication for surgery.

Correct. In stable atrial fibrillation the first goal is rate control and the second anticoagulation; outpatient cardioversion is done after 21 days of anticoagulation.
Adenosine treats or unmasks regular supraventricular tachycardia; it has no place before cardioversion of atrial fibrillation, which needs 21 days of anticoagulation.
Rate control is the first goal in atrial fibrillation and continues; what must precede outpatient cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation.

Committing to surgery is premature when imaging shows inflammatory, potentially reversible constriction in a stable patient.
Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade from fluid under pressure. Early inflammatory constriction is treated medically first.
A longer course of pericarditis drugs

Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Observation is unsafe with hypotension and confusion. Unstable Mobitz type II block is paced transcutaneously.
Correct. When medications are not used or do not work in unstable Mobitz type II block, the emergent measure is transcutaneous pacing, which bridges her to a permanent pacemaker.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. She has a pulse and a slow, blocked rhythm.
Synchronized cardioversion treats unstable tachycardias with a pulse. A slow rate from a failing conduction system needs pacing.

Catheterization shows normal coronary arteries. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with an outflow murmur. It does not produce transient apical hypokinesis after a stressor.
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a progressive global dilation with reduced squeeze over months, not a sudden regional apical weakness triggered by emotional stress.

Correct. A postmenopausal woman after an emotional stressor, with ST elevation, raised troponin, mid and apical hypokinesis and normal coronary arteries at catheterization, has Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy presents late with right-sided congestion and big atria. Sudden chest pain after grief with apical hypokinesis is stress cardiomyopathy.

Leriche syndrome is the aortoiliac triad of claudication, weak femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction. Digital atheroemboli cause blue toe syndrome.

Renal function is monitored during antibiotics, but harm reduction for injection drug use is addiction medicine's role.

Dermatology has no listed role; harm reduction for injection drug use comes from addiction medicine.

Children receive intravenous, not intramuscular, therapy, and doses are weight-based rather than fixed adult doses.

ruled out by a stated finding

ruled out by a stated finding
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with at least three P-wave shapes; an identical abnormal P wave before every QRS in a regular rhythm comes from a single focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 78-year-old woman has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, and her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block. Which of her conditions is singled out as a cause of this block?
opts: Tricuspid regurgitation is a right-sided holosystolic murmur. The valve lesion singled out for left bundle branch block is aortic stenosis.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Valvular heart disease, especially aortic stenosis, is a named cause of left bundle branch block, and her murmur is the classic aortic stenosis murmur.
Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic rumble at the apex, not this murmur, and is not singled out. Aortic stenosis is.
ruled out by a stated finding
Pulmonic stenosis loads the right ventricle and is heard at the left upper sternal border. Aortic stenosis is the lesion named.
ruled out by a stated finding

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 77-year-old man had cardiac surgery last year. A rhythm strip shows normal sinus beats, then a sudden pause with no P wave, after which narrow beats at 45 appear with no visible P waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus bradycardia is a regular rhythm under 60 with a P wave before every QRS, not a sudden pause followed by narrow beats with no P waves.
Atrial flutter shows rapid sawtooth waves at 250 or more, not a pause followed by slow narrow beats without P waves.
Sinus arrhythmia is a normal breathing-linked variation with a P wave before every beat, never a pause followed by junctional beats.

Correct. In sinus arrest the sinus node does not generate an impulse, leading to a junctional rhythm (narrow beats at 40 to 60 with no visible P waves); injury to the node from cardiac surgery is a listed cause.

A.q: Which electrical treatment is delivered for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a consistent QRS and suits unstable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse. Polymorphic rhythm is defibrillated.
Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms such as Mobitz type II and complete block. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with unsynchronized defibrillation.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, so there is no trial of drugs first: it is defibrillated, and an antiarrhythmic or beta blocker may be added afterward.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable and its QRS shape keeps changing, so it is defibrillated (unsynchronized) even when a pulse is present.

A.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
A.q: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve is booked for a diagnostic bronchoscopy. No biopsy or mucosal incision is planned. Which advice about endocarditis prophylaxis is most accurate?
opts: Plain bronchoscopy is on the list that does not need prophylaxis; only mucosal incision or biopsy changes that.
Vancomycin is not the standard prophylaxis and none is needed for this bronchoscopy.
Prophylaxis is never a week-long course, and none is needed for this bronchoscopy.
None is needed for this procedure
Correct. Bronchoscopy does not require prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the respiratory mucosa, such as a biopsy.

A.q: A 48-year-old woman started a medication known to prolong the QT interval last week. She now has palpitations but is awake and talking, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Beta blockers are avoided in torsades de pointes: the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly the QT.

Correct. A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose complexes twist around the baseline in a patient with a long QT is torsades de pointes; in a conscious patient intravenous magnesium breaks it, then more magnesium as an infusion.
Amiodarone (like procainamide) is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT further; magnesium is the treatment.
Adenosine treats regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia; this is a wide, polymorphic ventricular rhythm that needs magnesium.
A.alt: Rhythm strip of a rapid, wide-complex rhythm whose complexes grow taller, shrink, then grow again, as if turning around the baseline

A.q: How often is heart muscle biopsy useful in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: There is no surveillance biopsy. Biopsy is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy and is used only for defined indications.
Treatment does not wait for tissue. Biopsy is not used routinely in dilated cardiomyopathy and is kept for specific indications.
Correct. Biopsy is not used routinely and is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy; it is reserved for rapidly deteriorating function or systemic diseases that may involve the heart.
Biopsy is not needed to confirm dilated cardiomyopathy; the echocardiogram, electrocardiogram and imaging carry the diagnosis, and biopsy is rarely useful.

A.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: More adenosine blocks only the normal atrioventricular node and leaves the accessory pathway to carry the fibrillation; procainamide is used.

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is not repeated; adenosine and the other nodal blockers leave the accessory pathway unopposed.
Magnesium is for torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen a pre-excited tachycardia, which needs procainamide.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
A.q: A 38-year-old woman has three months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. Dilated cardiomyopathy is suspected, but her 12-lead electrocardiogram is completely normal. Which interpretation of the normal tracing is most accurate?
opts: It is what most dilated cardiomyopathy shows
The opposite holds: the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, with arrhythmias or conduction delay such as left bundle branch block.
It excludes every cause of heart failure
A normal electrocardiogram cannot exclude heart failure in general. The test that excludes heart failure is a B-type natriuretic peptide below 100 pg/mL.
It points to restrictive disease instead
Restrictive cardiomyopathy commonly shows atrial fibrillation, bundle branch blocks or low voltage in amyloidosis, so a normal tracing does not point toward it.
It makes dilated cardiomyopathy very unlikely

Correct. The electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, showing atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or left bundle branch block, so a normal tracing almost rules the diagnosis out.

A.q: A 64-year-old woman who smokes has cramping in her right calf after walking one block that eases after she stands still for several minutes. Her pedal pulses are diminished on the right. Which is the best initial test?
opts: Angiography is the invasive gold standard, used mainly to guide a planned intervention. It is not where the evaluation of new claudication begins; the ankle-brachial index is.
Magnetic resonance angiography is an alternative for patients with contrast allergy when an intervention is planned. The initial study is the ankle-brachial index at the bedside.
Computed tomography angiography needs contrast and is used mainly to plan an intervention. The first test for suspected disease is the bedside ankle-brachial index.
Correct. The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside test and the important initial test for suspected peripheral artery disease, comparing ankle to arm systolic pressure to grade severity.

A.q: A 17-year-old boy with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy asks his clinician what the most serious risk of his disease is. He has occasional palpitations and plays recreational basketball. Which complication is the leading cause of death in this condition?
opts: Heart failure symptoms gradually progress in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but sudden cardiac death, mostly from ventricular fibrillation, is the leading cause of mortality.
Aortic dissection is not a complication of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The leading cause of death is sudden cardiac death, usually from ventricular fibrillation.

Correct. Sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, highest in preadolescents and adolescents with extreme exertion, and over 80% of cases are associated with ventricular fibrillation.
Embolic stroke is a risk once atrial fibrillation develops, which is why anticoagulation is used. The leading cause of death is sudden cardiac death.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. A.q: A 30-year-old woman with known atrioventricular nodal reentry has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 178. She is stable. Which treatment almost always terminates it?
opts: Ablation offers a definitive cure for selected patients but is not how an acute episode is stopped.
Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required in nodal reentry and is kept for the unstable patient.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not nodal reentry.
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentry almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is rarely required.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
A.q: A 19-year-old man had a brief episode of racing heartbeat that stopped on its own. His resting electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke at the start of each QRS (delta wave). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A short PR interval with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) in sinus rhythm is pre-excitation from an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent): Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, with the potential for reentrant tachycardia.
Left bundle branch block widens the QRS with a dominant S wave in V1 and a normal PR; a short PR with a slurred upstroke is pre-excitation.
First-degree block lengthens the PR interval beyond 0.20 seconds; his PR is short, and the slurred QRS upstroke points to an accessory pathway.
Nodal reentry is a regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves during an episode; it does not leave a short PR and delta wave on the resting tracing.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
A.q: A 33-year-old man with typical acute pericarditis after a viral illness has a troponin that is above the reference range. Coronary angiography shows normal arteries. Which process does the troponin elevation most likely reflect?
opts: Correct. Troponin may be elevated if the myocardium is also affected, myopericarditis (perimyocarditis); an elevated troponin is also a feature that favors hospitalization.
There is no reason to dismiss the value; in pericarditis an elevated troponin is read as myocardial involvement.
His coronary arteries are normal, so troponin here reflects inflammation reaching the myocardium, not an occlusion.
ruled out by a stated finding
Constriction is a late, fibrotic process recognized by Kussmaul sign and imaging, not by troponin, which signals myocardial involvement.

A.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
A.q: A 61-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve has a fever of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) and Osler nodes (painful red nodules on the pads of her fingers). Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Osler nodes fall into?
opts: Her prosthetic valve is the predisposition; the Osler nodes themselves are an immunologic phenomenon.
Vascular phenomena include painless Janeway lesions and conjunctival hemorrhages; painful Osler nodes are immunologic.
Correct. Osler nodes are painful and immunologic; with glomerulonephritis, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor they make up the immunologic minor criterion.
The blood culture criterion needs cultures, not a skin finding. Osler nodes are a minor immunologic phenomenon.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 33-year-old man had a plaster cast removed from his right lower leg two days ago after a tibial fracture. He now has right calf swelling that measures 4 cm more than the left, and tenderness along the deep veins of the calf. Nothing else on the Wells criteria is present and no alternative diagnosis is as likely. What is his Wells score?
opts: One point undercounts. Each of his three positive items is worth 1 point, and none is offset by a likelier alternative diagnosis, which would subtract 2, so his total is three.
Two points would omit one positive item. The plaster immobilization, the calf swelling over 3 cm and the deep venous tenderness each score 1, so the total is three.

Correct. Recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremity, calf swelling over 3 cm and tenderness along the deep venous system are worth 1 point each, for 3. A score of 3 or more means high likelihood, so ultrasound is ordered.
Four points would need another positive item, such as pitting edema, swelling of the entire leg or active cancer, and he has none of these. His three findings total three.

A.q: A 71-year-old man with a new inferior myocardial infarction involving the right ventricle is hypotensive with distended jugular veins and clear lungs. Tamponade is considered. Why must his infarction stay on the differential?
opts: Infarction mimics acute tamponade; constriction, heart failure and cirrhosis mimic the subacute form.
Infarction is not the commonest cause of tamponade; it belongs here as a mimic and an occasional cause through rupture.
An infarction does not exclude tamponade; free-wall rupture after infarction can even cause it. It must be weighed as a mimic.
Correct. The differential of acute tamponade includes myocardial infarction (especially with right ventricular involvement), aortic dissection and massive pulmonary embolism, which can all mimic it.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
A.q: A 76-year-old man has had symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles for three weeks. He started amlodipine for hypertension one month ago. There is no warmth, redness, tenderness or skin discoloration, and he has no history of heart, kidney or liver disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Swelling that is often bilateral, without signs of inflammation, is a common adverse effect of some drugs, including dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine.
Lymphedema is chronic swelling, usually unilateral, often after pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation. This bilateral swelling began soon after starting a calcium channel blocker.
Deep vein thrombosis is usually unilateral and brings pain, warmth and erythema. Symmetric painless swelling that began after a new drug without inflammation fits medication-induced edema.
Chronic venous insufficiency produces brownish pigmentation, dermatitis and eventually ulceration after years of venous hypertension. Three weeks of bland swelling after a new drug does not fit.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 65-year-old woman developed chest pain and dyspnea during a hurricane evacuation. She has ST elevation, an elevated troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide, and an echocardiogram showing akinesis of the left ventricular apex. Which test confirms stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: Troponin is usually elevated in Takotsubo, just as in a heart attack, so it cannot separate them. Catheterization showing normal coronaries confirms it.
Exercise testing is inappropriate with active ST elevation and does not confirm the diagnosis. Cardiac catheterization with normal coronaries does.
Correct. The diagnosis of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries despite the infarct-like presentation.
Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not for stress cardiomyopathy. Catheterization with normal coronary arteries confirms Takotsubo.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: A 24-year-old man whose Wolff-Parkinson-White was found on a school electrocardiogram presents with palpitations. The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Atropine speeds conduction and is for unstable bradycardia; it would accelerate a pre-excited tachycardia.
Correct. Irregular, wide, very fast complexes in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White are pre-excited atrial fibrillation, treated with intravenous procainamide; adenosine must never be used.
Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a long QT, not pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Adenosine is contraindicated here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway carry the fibrillation.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
B.q: A 77-year-old woman is found unresponsive and pulseless, and chest compressions are started. Her monitor strip is shown, and the same flat tracing appears in every lead. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Defibrillation treats ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia; asystole and pulseless electrical activity are unshockable.
Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS complex to time the shock to and a patient with a pulse; asystole has neither and is unshockable.

Correct. A flat line with no P waves or QRS complexes is asystole, which is unshockable: continue high-quality chest compressions and give epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes, the mainstays of treatment; the prognosis is poor.
Amiodarone is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia that persists after shocks; asystole is treated with compressions and epinephrine.
B.alt: Rhythm strip with a nearly flat line across the whole page and no complexes

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
B.q: A 55-year-old man has a positive D-dimer during evaluation of calf pain two weeks after a bicycle crash with extensive bruising. He asks why his clinician says the result cannot confirm a clot. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: It reflects fibrinolysis from many causes

Correct. D-dimer elevation implies increased fibrinolysis, but it is sensitive and not specific. Bruising, surgery, cancer and many other conditions raise it, so a positive result needs imaging while a negative one helps rule out a clot.
It rises only with pulmonary embolism
D-dimer rises with fibrinolysis anywhere in the body, including after trauma, and is useful as a rule-out test for both deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It is not limited to one disease.
It is specific but not sensitive
This reverses the facts: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. Its sensitivity is why a negative result helps rule out a clot, and its poor specificity is why a positive one needs imaging.
It rises only with thigh clots
D-dimer does not localize a clot to the thigh or anywhere else. It reflects fibrinolysis from many causes, so ultrasound is needed to find and locate any thrombus.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: Which is a risk factor for multiple recurrences of pericarditis?
opts: severe late gadolinium enhancement predicts multiple recurrences; mild uptake is the reassuring end of that scale.
It is a high C-reactive protein, by magnitude of elevation, that predicts multiple recurrences, not a low one.
A prompt recovery from viral pericarditis is a good sign. An autoimmune etiology predicts multiple recurrences.
Correct. Risk factors for multiple recurrences are the magnitude of C-reactive protein elevation, the severity of pericardial late gadolinium enhancement and an autoimmune etiology.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: What causes the pain of a pseudoaneurysm?
opts: Correct. A pseudoaneurysm presents with pain from increased pressure due to swelling, or from nerve compression, at the site of the arterial leak.
An intimal tear gives the tearing pain of dissection. Pseudoaneurysm pain comes from swelling or nerve compression.
Walking-induced muscle ischemia is claudication. Pseudoaneurysm pain comes from swelling or nerve compression.
Retroperitoneal bleeding marks a ruptured abdominal aneurysm. Pseudoaneurysm pain is from swelling or nerve compression.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
B.q: Why is a patient with cardiomyopathy referred to cardiology?
opts: Only once symptoms occur at rest
Referral does not wait for symptoms at rest. It establishes care, considers genetic testing and reviews high-risk features early.
Only when a device must be implanted
Device decisions are one reason, but referral also establishes care, considers genetic testing and reviews high-risk features.
To establish care and review risk features
Correct. Referral is to establish care, consider genetic testing, review any high-risk features, and discuss medications or the need for an intervention.
Only after an admission for edema
An admission is not required first. Cardiology referral is made to establish care and review risk, testing and treatment options.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
B.q: A 55-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has 2 days of worsening dyspnea and chest discomfort. Blood pressure is 84/56, heart rate 122, jugular veins are distended, and heart sounds are muffled. Her blood pressure drops by 18 mmHg on inspiration (pulsus paradoxus, an inspiratory drop in blood pressure). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Constriction develops over months with edema, ascites and the Kussmaul sign; it does not cause this acute hypotension with muffled sounds.
Tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation; muffled heart sounds with pulsus paradoxus point to tamponade.

Correct. Hypotension, distended jugular veins and muffled heart sounds (the Beck triad) with pulsus paradoxus and tachycardia in a patient with malignancy are cardiac tamponade, pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart.
Acute pericarditis causes sharp positional pain and a rub; on its own it does not cause hypotension, jugular distension and pulsus paradoxus.

B.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
B.q: A 47-year-old man who injects drugs has a fever of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F) and Janeway lesions (painless hemorrhagic macules) on the soles of both feet. Blood cultures are pending. Under the modified Duke criteria, which category do the Janeway lesions fall into?
opts: Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor. Painless Janeway lesions are vascular.

Correct. Janeway lesions are a vascular (embolic) phenomenon, a minor criterion with major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage and conjunctival hemorrhages.
Microbiologic evidence is a culture or serologic finding; the cultures here are still pending.
ruled out by a stated finding
Major endocardial evidence comes from echocardiography or new valvular regurgitation, not from skin lesions.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: A 67-year-old woman has had 2 months of low-grade fevers to 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), fatigue and a 4-kilogram weight loss. She had a tooth extracted 10 weeks ago. A new apical systolic murmur is heard, and splinter hemorrhages (thin dark lines under the nail plates) are seen on two fingers. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tuberculosis causes fever, night sweats and weight loss, but not a new murmur with splinter hemorrhages after dental work.
Acute disease is abrupt and toxic over 3-10 days with high fevers. Two months of low-grade fever and weight loss is subacute.

Correct. An indolent course with lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks to months, a new murmur, splinter hemorrhages and a dental source fits subacute endocarditis, classically from viridans streptococci.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia with high inflammatory markers; it does not produce a new murmur or splinter hemorrhages.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. B.q: A 52-year-old man has a cardiac arrest after choking on food at a restaurant. The obstruction is removed, but he remains pulseless with an organized rhythm on the monitor. Compressions are underway. Which airway step should be considered early?
opts: Correct. Pulseless electrical activity is unshockable; compressions start at once and intubation is considered early, since hypoxia is one of its two leading causes.
An organized pulseless rhythm is unshockable. Early intubation addresses the hypoxia that caused it.
ruled out by a stated finding
A bronchodilator does not secure the airway. Early intubation addresses his hypoxia.
Airway support is not delayed until a pulse returns; intubation is considered early.

B.q: A 62-year-old man with fever has four sets of blood cultures drawn. One set grows coagulase-negative staphylococci, and the other three are negative. How should this single positive culture be counted under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: As the major blood culture criterion
The major criterion needs a typical organism in two separate cultures or persistent bacteremia, not one culture of a common contaminant.
Correct. Single positive cultures for coagulase-negative staphylococci (and diphtheroids) are excluded from the microbiologic criterion because they are common culture contaminants.
Vascular phenomena are embolic findings such as Janeway lesions, not culture results.
One culture of a common contaminant proves nothing; it is excluded from the criteria.

B.q: A 60-year-old man who smokes has a 4.3 cm asymptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysm and a blood pressure of 158/94. He asks what he can do to help himself. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Management of a thoracic aortic aneurysm includes smoking cessation, beta-adrenergic blockers and aggressive blood pressure control, with surveillance imaging for his size.
Smoking matters only for leg disease
Smoking cessation is listed first in thoracic aneurysm management. Continuing to smoke works against him.
Blood pressure matters only after surgery
Aggressive blood pressure control is part of management now, before any surgery. Hypertension is common in patients with thoracic aneurysm.
Medical management starts at diagnosis: stop smoking, beta blockade and aggressive blood pressure control, alongside surveillance.

B.q: A 74-year-old man with sudden leg ischemia has sensory loss extending beyond the toes with rest pain, mild-to-moderate weakness, an inaudible arterial Doppler signal and an audible venous signal. Where should his evaluation and treatment take place?
opts: Time for imaging such as computed tomography angiography belongs to viable or marginally threatened limbs. An immediately threatened limb goes to the surgical suite.
Amputation is for irreversible limbs with profound sensory loss, paralysis and absent venous signals. This limb is still salvageable with immediate revascularization.
In the surgical suite, without delay
Correct. An immediately threatened limb is salvageable only with immediate revascularization, so it should preferentially undergo further evaluation and treatment in a surgical suite.
Outpatient testing wastes the time this limb does not have. Sensory loss beyond the toes with weakness means immediate revascularization in a surgical suite.

B.q: Which history typically accompanies lymphedema when it mimics deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Long flights raise clot risk through stasis but do not explain chronic edema. Lymphedema usually follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation.
Starting a new blood pressure drug
A new drug causes edema that is often bilateral, without inflammation, which is drug-induced edema. Lymphedema usually follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation.
Correct. Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually with a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy that damaged lymphatic drainage.
An inciting injury with bruising at the ankle suggests a calf muscle tear. Lymphedema usually follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation.

B.q: A 52-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a rhythm strip in which a normal beat is followed by an early beat with an abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS, repeating so that every other beat is early (bigeminy). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A junctional rhythm is a steady slow rhythm at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves, not alternating early beats.
Flutter shows continuous sawtooth waves at 250 or more, not alternating normal and early beats.
Premature ventricular beats are early, wide and bizarre with no P wave; hers have abnormal P waves and narrow QRS complexes.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Early beats with an abnormal P wave and narrow QRS are premature atrial contractions (common in chronic lung disease), and an ectopic beat every other beat is bigeminy.

B.q: Which history precedes viral myocarditis?
opts: Trauma is not the setting. The history is a flulike viral prodrome in the 1 to 2 weeks before heart failure symptoms.
A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks before
Correct. Viral myocarditis follows a recent (1 to 2 week) flulike syndrome with fever, myalgia, fatigue, respiratory symptoms or gastroenteritis before the heart failure symptoms.
An emotional stressor precedes stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy. Viral myocarditis follows a flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier.
Long-term excess alcohol causes dilated cardiomyopathy. Viral myocarditis follows a recent flulike illness.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: A 39-year-old woman who injects drugs has native valve endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is treated with vancomycin or daptomycin, the key difference from susceptible strains being vancomycin in place of a penicillin.
Nafcillin and oxacillin treat methicillin-susceptible strains; resistant strains need vancomycin or daptomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ampicillin with gentamicin is an enterococcal regimen and does not treat methicillin-resistant staphylococci.
Cefazolin treats methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus; it does not cover resistant strains.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 71-year-old man has been on strict bed rest for six days during an admission for pneumonia and now has swelling and aching of the entire left leg. Which component of the Virchow triad does his prolonged bed rest represent?
opts: Endothelial trauma is direct injury to the vein wall from surgery, fracture, burns, catheters or injection. Bed rest for pneumonia does not injure the vessel lining; it slows flow, which is stasis.

A hypercoagulable state is an inherited or acquired clotting tendency, such as factor V Leiden, cancer, estrogen use or pregnancy. Lying still changes blood flow rather than clotting chemistry, so it is stasis.
Arterial vasospasm is not a component of the Virchow triad, which comprises venous stasis, hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma. Immobility acts on the veins by slowing their blood flow.

Correct. Bed rest is immobilization, which alters blood flow and lets blood pool in the leg veins, the venous stasis component of the Virchow triad. Prolonged immobilization raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis about twenty-fold.

B.q: A 26-year-old woman with asthma used her inhaler repeatedly during an attack and then felt a sudden, rapid pounding in her chest. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves. Which factor most likely triggered this rhythm?
opts: Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome; it slows the heart rather than triggering a reentrant tachycardia.
Increased vagal tone slows conduction and appears among the causes of junctional rhythm and first-degree block, not of a sudden fast rhythm.
Low potassium is a listed cause of premature ventricular contractions and of acquired long QT; this narrow, regular tachycardia with hidden P waves is nodal reentry.

Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with hidden P waves in a young woman is nodal reentrant tachycardia, which may start spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics.

B.q: What makes up atheroemboli?
opts: Marrow fat is not the material described. Atheroemboli are fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques.
Air is not part of atheroembolism. The emboli are fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from plaques.
Clot formed in the left atrium
Atrial clot gives thromboemboli, the usual cause of acute limb ischemia. Atheroemboli are fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris.
Correct. Atheroembolism is multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris embolizing from proximal atherosclerotic lesions.

B.q: A 70-year-old woman on telemetry has torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline). The first-line intravenous push broke the first run, but short runs keep recurring. She is alert with a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: She is stable, and a polymorphic rhythm cannot be synchronized. Recurrent runs get a magnesium infusion.
Correct. Torsades in a conscious patient is broken with intravenous magnesium and then treated with more magnesium as an infusion: magnesium, and more magnesium.
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. A magnesium infusion follows the first push.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Recurrent runs are treated with a magnesium infusion.

B.q: A 69-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted in an acute exacerbation. She is tachycardic and irregular, and her electrocardiogram shows three or more different P-wave shapes in one lead with a P wave before each QRS. Which is the most important treatment for this rhythm?
opts: Correct. Management of multifocal atrial tachycardia is treating the underlying condition, here the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation; short-term rate control may be added in hospital.
Adenosine is for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia through the atrioventricular node; it does not treat multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Ablation is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia, not for a multifocal rhythm driven by acute lung disease.
Cardioversion does not stop several independent atrial foci; treating the underlying lung disease does.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
B.q: In sick sinus syndrome, a fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves alternates with pauses. Which rhythm is the fast run?
opts: Correct. An irregularly irregular fast rhythm with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, and in tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which fast and slow rhythms alternate, atrial fibrillation is the most common tachyarrhythmia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but every QRS has a P wave, in at least three shapes; a fast run with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
ruled out by a stated finding
Sinus tachycardia is regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS; in tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in a few patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but it is regular and wide; an irregularly irregular run without P waves is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 62-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy through a central venous catheter has two days of right arm swelling and aching. The catheter injuring the vein wall is the endothelial trauma component of the Virchow triad. Which is the best diagnostic test?
opts: The ankle-brachial index compares ankle and arm pressures to detect peripheral artery disease in the legs. It does not evaluate a swollen arm for a venous clot.
Contrast ascending venography was the gold standard but is invasive and has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound. It is not the first test for a catheter-related arm clot.
D-dimer is nonspecific and is often elevated in cancer, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot and cannot replace imaging. Venous duplex ultrasound is the test that shows the thrombus.

Correct. Venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity is the diagnostic test for deep vein thrombosis, including arm clots from central venous catheters. It has replaced venography, the old invasive gold standard.

B.q: A 52-year-old man is discharged after a large viral pericardial effusion was found without tamponade. He asks how the effusion will be monitored. Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
opts: Radiographs show only gross enlargement. Serial echocardiograms are the follow-up for large effusions.
Large effusions can reaccumulate; serial echocardiograms are recommended even when symptoms settle.
Correct. All large pericardial effusions should be followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms, with close clinical follow-up by the specialty matching the cause.
An electrocardiogram cannot measure fluid. Serial transthoracic echocardiograms follow a large effusion.

B.q: A 19-year-old woman has had three episodes of a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 230 that converted with adenosine. Her tracing in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave). Which is the first-line long-term treatment?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; an accessory pathway is cured by catheter ablation.
Oral beta blockers or calcium channel blockers are the initial long-term therapy for focal atrial tachycardia; for Wolff-Parkinson-White, ablation of the pathway is first line.
A pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or calcium channel blocker is an option for nodal reentrant tachycardia; Wolff-Parkinson-White is treated by ablating the pathway.
Correct. A short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) marks Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line long-term treatment.

B.q: A 58-year-old man collapses in a gym. He is unresponsive, not breathing and has no pulse. The monitor shows chaotic, irregular waves of varying size with no identifiable QRS complexes. Which rhythm is present?
opts: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia still has identifiable, if varying, QRS complexes. Chaotic waves without any QRS are fibrillation.
Correct. Uncoordinated electrical activity with no rate, no P waves and no organized QRS, in a pulseless patient, is ventricular fibrillation.
Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. Chaotic waves mean ventricular fibrillation.
Pulseless electrical activity shows an organized rhythm without a pulse. This rhythm is chaotic.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. B.q: A 65-year-old woman with lung cancer has a moderate effusion, dyspnea and a blood pressure of 100/68. Her clinician measures her blood pressure through the respiratory cycle. Which result most supports tamponade?
opts: Blood pressure drops, not rises, with inspiration in tamponade; pulsus paradoxus is a 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure with inspiration.
Correct. Pulsus paradoxus, a 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure with inspiration, is a physical finding of both acute and subacute tamponade, along with an elevated jugular venous pressure.
An unchanged pressure does not suggest tamponade, where pulsus paradoxus brings a 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure with inspiration.
A 4 mmHg drop falls short of the 10 mmHg inspiratory drop in blood pressure that marks pulsus paradoxus in tamponade.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
B.q: A 63-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy comes to clinic with mild breathlessness on exertion. Her examination shows trace ankle edema and clear lungs. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 60 pg/mL. What does this natriuretic peptide result indicate?
opts: Myocarditis is established by endomyocardial biopsy once other causes are excluded; a natriuretic peptide does not confirm it, and her level is below the 100 pg/mL cut-off that makes heart failure unlikely.
An elevated B-type natriuretic peptide indicates raised left ventricular filling pressure and dysfunction. A level of 60 pg/mL is below 100, which makes heart failure unlikely rather than confirmed.

Correct. B-type natriuretic peptide is released when ventricular filling pressures are high, and a level below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure an unlikely explanation for her current symptoms, although a low level does not strictly rule it out.
Raised filling pressure releases B-type natriuretic peptide and pushes the level up. A result under 100 pg/mL points the other way and makes heart failure an unlikely explanation.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
B.q: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden, severe, ripping chest pain. His electrocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: The ankle-brachial index grades leg arterial disease. Suspected dissection is imaged with computed tomography of the chest and abdomen.
Reassure him; the tracing is normal
A normal electrocardiogram is common in aortic dissection and does not rule it out. Sudden tearing pain needs computed tomography of the chest and abdomen.
Correct. The electrocardiogram may be normal in aortic dissection, so a normal tracing does not exclude it; computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent of the dissection.
A plain film cannot show an intimal tear or false lumen. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
B.q: What is the prognosis of viridans streptococcal infective endocarditis?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism; viridans streptococci carry a relatively good prognosis if treated before complications.
Correct. Viridans streptococcal endocarditis has a relatively good prognosis if antibiotic treatment is started before complications occur.
A 30-40% valve-replacement rate is described for enterococcal endocarditis, not viridans streptococci.
Prompt treatment is what makes the outlook relatively good: viridans streptococcal endocarditis does well if antibiotics start before complications.

B.q: A 26-year-old marathon runner has a resting heart rate of 48 at a preparticipation physical. He denies dizziness, fainting or chest pain. The electrocardiogram shows a regular rhythm with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR interval of 0.16 seconds. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia; this athlete's adaptive bradycardia causes no symptoms.
Training explains the slow rate and is not harmful here; asymptomatic sinus bradycardia in an athlete needs only reassurance.
Correct. Sinus bradycardia is seen in healthy people as an adaptive response, particularly well-conditioned athletes, and an asymptomatic sinus bradycardia is not treated.
Atropine is first line only for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; a well, conditioned runner needs no drug.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. B.q: A 79-year-old woman is brought in after fainting. Her pulse is 34. Her electrocardiogram shows regular P waves at 80 and regular wide QRS complexes at 34, with no fixed relationship between them. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus bradycardia has a P wave before every QRS with a normal PR; her atrial rate is 80 while the ventricles beat at 34, unrelated.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. P waves and QRS complexes at two separate regular rates with no association is complete dissociation of the atria from the ventricles: third-degree (complete) block, with a ventricular rate usually under 40.
A junctional rhythm is regular and narrow at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves; she has regular upright P waves at 80 running separately from a wide rhythm at 34.
Mobitz type II conducts most P waves with a constant PR and drops an occasional QRS; here no P wave has a fixed relation to any QRS.

B.q: A 30-year-old cyclist with no symptoms has a rhythm in which the PR interval lengthens beat by beat until a QRS complex is dropped, after which the cycle starts again. Echocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing is an emergency bridge for unstable high-grade block. Stable, silent Mobitz type I needs no treatment.
Correct. Asymptomatic Mobitz type I block needs no treatment; a permanent pacemaker is considered only for debilitating symptoms or heart failure symptoms.
A pacemaker is for symptomatic Mobitz type I, or for Mobitz type II even without symptoms. A symptom-free cyclist needs no treatment.
Ablation destroys conduction tissue and is itself a named cause of Mobitz type I. A silent block needs no treatment.

B.q: A 38-year-old woman has long-standing swelling of both legs just above the ankles that is symmetric, with normal skin color and no ulcers or varicose veins. Cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lymphedema presents with unilateral swelling, no varicosities and pitting edema. Symmetric bilateral swelling just above the ankles in a woman describes lipedema.
Insufficiency brings pitting edema with brown pigmentation, dermatitis or ulcers from venous hypertension. Her skin is normal and there are no varicose veins, so lipedema fits better.

Correct. Bilateral, symmetric swelling just above the ankles in a woman, with normal cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations and no venous skin changes, is the description of lipedema in the differential of leg edema.
Heart failure also swells both legs but comes with cardiac findings, and her cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. Symmetric swelling above the ankles is lipedema.

B.q: A 48-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is admitted after surgery with low blood pressure, and a resident proposes a drug to strengthen her heart's contraction. Which drug class should be avoided in her?
opts: Correct. Positive inotropes such as digoxin, epinephrine and norepinephrine are avoided because the increased contractility worsens outflow obstruction, raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias.
Amiodarone reduces the risk of sudden cardiac death and converts atrial fibrillation in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Positive inotropes are the class to avoid.
Beta blockers are the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, reducing contractility and improving filling. They are not the class to avoid.
Verapamil and diltiazem treat outflow obstruction by slowing the heart and reducing contractility. Drugs that increase contractility are the ones avoided.
