B.q: A 48-year-old woman with known pulmonary sarcoidosis faints at work. She takes no medications. Her heart rate is 35, and the electrocardiogram shows P waves at a regular rate with no relationship to slow QRS complexes. Which named cause of her block fits her best?
opts: Increased vagal tone causes first-degree and Mobitz type I block at the node, not complete block with fainting. Her known sarcoidosis, an infiltrative disease, is a named cause of complete block.

Correct. Inflammatory and infiltrative disease (myocarditis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis) is a named cause of complete heart block; at 48, infiltration of the heart by her known sarcoidosis, a granulomatous disease, is the explanation that fits.
Degeneration of the conduction system is the most common cause overall, especially in old age, but at 48 with known sarcoidosis the infiltrative disease is the more likely cause.
She takes no medications, so a drug effect is ruled out. Sarcoidosis, an infiltrative disease, is a named cause of complete heart block.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 55-year-old man has progressive breathlessness on exertion, fatigue and swelling of both legs. The apical impulse is displaced laterally, a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is present, and there is a soft murmur at the apex. Which echocardiogram finding would support dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Normal cavity size with large atria and stiff walls
A near-normal cavity with marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function is restrictive cardiomyopathy, where systolic function is usually preserved.
Dilated thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction

Correct. Dilated, thin walls are the prominent echocardiogram feature, with an ejection fraction below 40%, hypokinetic chambers, possibly all four chambers dilated, mitral or tricuspid regurgitation and sometimes thrombus.
Hypokinesis confined to the mid and apical segments is the transient regional pattern of stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, not global dilation.
A thick septum and a small left ventricular cavity
Asymmetric septal thickening with a small cavity is the echocardiogram of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where the ejection fraction is normal or even high.

B.q: An 86-year-old woman with end-stage cardiomyopathy has breathlessness at rest, edema and fatigue despite maximal tolerated therapy. She is not a transplant or device candidate and says she wants comfort at home. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: She is not a transplant candidate and has asked for comfort at home. End-stage cardiomyopathy in this setting calls for goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral.
She is not a device candidate, and her stated goal is comfort at home. Advance care planning and hospice referral match end-stage disease here.
Stop all of her symptom medicines
Palliative care actively manages dyspnea, fatigue and edema; it does not withdraw symptom relief. The step now is goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral.
Discuss goals of care and hospice

Correct. Palliative care in cardiomyopathy covers symptom management of dyspnea, fatigue and edema, advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions, support for caregivers, and hospice referral in end-stage disease.

B.q: How is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia treated, even when the patient has a pulse?
opts: Drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never stable and is defibrillated.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state, so it is defibrillated even if the patient looks well.
Synchronized shocks need a consistent QRS to time against. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated, even with a pulse.
Watching is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a transitional state that needs defibrillation.

B.q: A 71-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve is having a gum biopsy. She is not allergic to penicillin, but she cannot swallow pills after a recent stroke. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
A prosthetic valve is high risk, and a biopsy perforates the oral mucosa, so prophylaxis is indicated.
ruled out by a stated finding
She cannot take oral medication, so the oral amoxicillin standard is not possible; ampicillin by injection is used.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A patient without penicillin allergy who cannot take oral medication receives ampicillin intramuscularly or intravenously (or cefazolin or ceftriaxone) 30-60 minutes before.

B.q: A 66-year-old woman with ovarian cancer has had three drainages for a recurrent pericardial effusion, and the latest echocardiogram shows a loculated collection behind the heart. Which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. A pericardiectomy or pericardial window is performed for recurrent effusions and for loculated effusions, especially posterior ones that cannot be approached percutaneously.
A posterior loculated collection cannot be reached percutaneously, and repeat taps fail with recurrence; a window is needed.
Thoracentesis drains the pleural space, not the pericardium. A pericardial window is the procedure.
Diuretics do not drain a malignant loculated effusion. A pericardial window does.

B.q: A 64-year-old woman with heart failure has had a regular, wide-complex tachycardia at 150 for 40 minutes, every QRS the same shape. She is alert, with no chest pain or shortness of breath and a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) is for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation; she is alert with a pulse and a normal blood pressure, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion.

Correct. Regular wide complexes of one shape for over 30 seconds are sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen with heart failure; she is hemodynamically stable, so the treatment is pharmacologic cardioversion with an intravenous antiarrhythmic such as amiodarone.
Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic tachycardia of a long QT; her complexes are all one shape, so this is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse (chest pain, confusion, dyspnea, hypotension); she has none of these, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion.

B.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations after three energy drinks. She notices her neck throbbing, and examination shows a frog sign (rapid visible pulsations in the neck). Her heart rate is 172 and regular, with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A paroxysmal, regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves, neck pulsations (the frog sign) and a stimulant trigger in a young woman without heart disease is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three or more P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients.
Sinus tachycardia shows a normal P wave before each QRS and rarely exceeds 160; hers has hidden P waves at 172 with sudden onset.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; her rhythm is regular, which points to nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 35-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy developed severe asthma symptoms when a beta blocker was started, and it was stopped. She still has exertional breathlessness from outflow obstruction. Which medication is the appropriate alternative?
opts: Norepinephrine is a positive inotrope that increases contractility and may induce arrhythmias, so it is avoided. The alternative to a beta blocker is verapamil or diltiazem.
Nifedipine is a dihydropyridine that mainly vasodilates. Lowering afterload worsens outflow obstruction; the calcium channel blockers used are verapamil and diltiazem.
Nitrates reduce preload and afterload and aggravate outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Verapamil or diltiazem is the alternative.

Correct. The nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers verapamil and diltiazem are the listed alternative to a beta blocker for outflow tract obstruction, slowing the heart and reducing contractility.

B.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A normal P wave before every narrow QRS at 60 to 100, with the rate rising on inspiration and falling on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia: a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern.
Sick sinus syndrome produces pauses, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings in a diseased node, usually with symptoms; a breathing-linked variation in a healthy swimmer is sinus arrhythmia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast, irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients; her single P-wave shape at 72 is sinus.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; she has a normal P wave before every beat and a regular pattern tied to breathing.

B.q: A 71-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and a reduced ejection fraction has worsening dyspnea and fatigue despite medical therapy. His electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.16 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic R waves in I, V5 and V6. Which is the most appropriate treatment for this conduction problem?
opts: Catheter ablation treats accessory pathways, focal atrial tachycardia and some ventricular rhythms; a symptomatic left bundle branch block with low ejection fraction gets biventricular pacing.
Most left bundle branch block is left untreated, but symptomatic block with reduced ejection fraction is the exception that gets a biventricular pacemaker.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; left bundle branch block is a conduction delay in sinus rhythm, treated here with a biventricular pacemaker.

Correct. A wide QRS with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic lateral R waves is left bundle branch block; it is usually left untreated, except symptomatic block with reduced ejection fraction, which gets a biventricular pacemaker.

B.q: A 58-year-old man who takes a beta blocker has an irregular pulse at a routine visit. He has no symptoms, and his rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Third-degree block shows no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes; here the conducted beats keep a PR interval that lengthens in a repeating pattern.
First-degree block is a long but constant PR with every P wave conducted; this strip has a P wave that is not followed by a QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding
Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR interval before randomly dropped QRS complexes; on this strip the PR lengthens progressively before each drop.

Correct. The PR interval grows longer beat by beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle restarts: second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block, which medications such as beta blockers can cause.
B.alt: Rhythm strip with small upright P waves and narrow complexes in groups, with a gap where one P wave stands alone

B.q: A 70-year-old man with a recent transient ischemic attack has a high-grade carotid stenosis on duplex and is being prepared for intervention. Which study is considered the gold standard?
opts: Correct. Digital subtraction angiography is an invasive angiographic technique considered the gold standard; it is not used for screening but for guiding therapeutic interventions.
Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial screening and monitoring tool. The gold standard used to guide intervention is digital subtraction angiography.
Magnetic resonance angiography images the cervical and intracranial circulation and brain very effectively. The gold standard, however, is digital subtraction angiography.
A bruit is an examination finding, auscultated one side at a time with the breath held. It cannot grade stenosis; digital subtraction angiography is the gold standard.

B.q: A 24-year-old soccer player comes to urgent care with left calf pain that began two days ago when he felt a sudden pull while sprinting, and he has bruising around the ankle. He has no leg swelling, tenderness along the deep veins, cancer, cast or history of clots. By the Wells criteria, a calf muscle tear is at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis. Which is the most appropriate first test?
opts: Contrast ascending venography is invasive and has been replaced by duplex ultrasound. It is not an initial test for a low-likelihood patient, whose first step is a D-dimer.

Venous duplex ultrasound is ordered first for a high Wells score, or after a positive D-dimer. For this low-likelihood patient it is not the first test, because a negative D-dimer could end the work-up.
Computed tomography of the leg is not part of the deep vein thrombosis pathway, which relies on the D-dimer for low-likelihood patients and venous duplex ultrasound for confirmation.

Correct. The likelier alternative diagnosis subtracts 2 from his Wells score, giving a low likelihood. Low-likelihood patients start with a D-dimer, and a negative result lets the clinician stop, since D-dimer is a sensitive rule-out test.

B.q: A 67-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has palpitations and dyspnea. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 150, with two sawtooth atrial waves before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Focal atrial tachycardia has one abnormal P wave per QRS from a single focus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is the 2:1 block of atrial flutter.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no organized atrial waves; her rhythm is regular with repeating sawtooth waves.
Sinus tachycardia has one upright P wave before each QRS; she has two identical sawtooth waves for every QRS.

Correct. Sawtooth atrial waves outnumbering the QRS complexes, here two to one (the most common block), make atrial flutter, which is common with pulmonary vascular disease or right-sided heart failure.

B.q: A 55-year-old woman taking a loop diuretic for heart failure has new palpitations felt in her neck. Telemetry shows frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which laboratory values should be checked first?
opts: Thyroid and adrenal tests are not the first step. Premature ventricular contractions call for potassium and magnesium levels.
These look for infarction and pancreatitis. Frequent premature beats on a diuretic call for potassium and magnesium.
Correct. Electrolyte imbalances, especially hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia (with hypercalcemia), are main causes of premature ventricular contractions, and a loop diuretic can lower both.
Glucose and lactate are not the named triggers. Low potassium and low magnesium are.

B.q: A 52-year-old man has had 10 days of gradually worsening pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain without a clear onset. His temperature is 38.7 degrees Celsius (101.7 degrees Fahrenheit), and the echocardiogram shows a moderate pericardial effusion without collapse of any chamber. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Pericardiectomy is for recurrent or loculated effusions and constriction, not a first presentation. He needs admission and workup.
Reassurance and repeat echo in 3 months
Waiting months with fever and a moderate effusion is unsafe; these high-risk features call for admission and evaluation now.
His fever above 38 degrees Celsius, subacute course and moderate effusion are each associated with higher risk and a potential need for hospitalization.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Fever above 38 degrees Celsius, a subacute course over days to weeks and a moderate to large effusion are all high-risk features that favor hospitalization and further evaluation.

B.q: A 38-year-old woman has a congenital arteriovenous fistula of the calf with numerous small communications, causing chronic swelling and aching. She has no signs of ischemia or heart failure. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Ligating each communication is impractical because the connections can be numerous. Conservative treatment with elastic support hose is the standard initial approach.
Surgical removal or size reduction suits an acquired fistula. Congenital fistulas have numerous communications, making excision difficult, so conservative care is used first.

Correct. Congenital fistulas are difficult to treat because the communications can be numerous, so they are managed conservatively with elastic support hose once peripheral artery disease is excluded. Embolization sometimes removes one.
Anticoagulation treats venous thrombosis and does not close or manage an artery to vein connection. Congenital fistulas are treated conservatively with elastic support hose.

B.q: What adjustment is suggested for colchicine in older adults with pericarditis?
opts: Colchicine is an oral drug and no intravenous route is suggested. The adjustment is a dose reduction.
Lengthening the course is not the adjustment. Colchicine is considered for dose reduction in older adults.
Correct. Older adults call for caution with anti-inflammatory therapy, and colchicine should be considered for dose reduction, as it should for lower body weight.
Colchicine remains part of therapy; it is considered for dose reduction in older adults rather than avoided.

B.q: After parenteral therapy for 5 days, which agents can anticoagulation be switched to?
opts: These make up the classical bridging strategy, where heparin overlaps warfarin. The switch after 5 days of parenteral therapy is to dabigatran or edoxaban.
Antiplatelet drugs are not anticoagulants for deep vein thrombosis. The switch after parenteral therapy is to dabigatran or edoxaban.
These are used as oral monotherapy with a loading dose followed by maintenance, without a parenteral lead-in. The switch after 5 days is to dabigatran or edoxaban.

B.q: A 40-year-old man has a stable, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 180. It is unclear whether the rhythm comes from a focus in the atria or a reentry circuit that uses the atrioventricular node. Which agent is most useful as a diagnostic tool?
opts: Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, but it does not separate an atrial focus from a node-dependent circuit; adenosine does.

Correct. Adenosine is an important diagnostic tool here: it usually terminates reentry that depends on the atrioventricular node but is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia, so the response separates them.
Procainamide is used for atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway; adenosine, not procainamide, is the diagnostic tool for a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
Magnesium treats torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular rhythm with a long QT; it has no diagnostic role in a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.

B.q: A 69-year-old woman with claudication, a known contrast allergy and reduced renal function needs arterial imaging before a planned intervention. Which study is relatively contraindicated for her?
opts: Magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative for patients with contrast allergy. Its classic barriers are pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips, which she does not have.
The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside cuff test with no contrast at all. It is the important initial test and carries no risk for her kidneys.

Correct. Computed tomography angiography uses contrast to show arterial anatomy, and contrast allergy and decreased renal function are relative contraindications, cautions that steer her toward another study; she has both.
Duplex ultrasound is noninvasive and uses no contrast media or radiation, so it is safe here. It is the mainstay initial imaging when stenosis is suspected.

B.q: A 57-year-old man with constrictive pericarditis is scheduled for pericardiectomy next week. He takes a loop diuretic for leg edema. How should the diuretic be handled before surgery?
opts: Correct. If surgery is planned, diuretics should be used sparingly in the preoperative period, even though they relieve the fluid overload of constriction.
Aggressive diuresis before pericardiectomy is advised against; diuretics are used sparingly preoperatively.
No route change is recommended; the guidance for the preoperative period is to use diuretics sparingly.
Adding diuretics intensifies volume depletion before surgery. Diuretics should be used sparingly.

Mapping and ablation are a later option in atrial fibrillation; the first goal in a stable patient is rate control, then anticoagulation.
Synchronized cardioversion now is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation; she is alert and normotensive, so rate control comes first.

B.q: An 81-year-old man takes no medications and has never had a heart attack. A routine electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.25 seconds with every beat conducted, and he asks why his heart is doing this. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: Lyme carditis is a named cause, but without exposure or a rash the leading explanation in an older man is degeneration of the conduction system.
Correct. The most common cause of first-degree atrioventricular block is age-related degenerative change of the conduction system, so the impulse takes longer to cross the atrioventricular node.
Increased vagal tone is a named cause, typically in young, well-conditioned people. In an 81-year-old, age-related degeneration is the usual cause.
Hidden damage from a heart attack
Atrioventricular node ischemia usually follows a myocardial infarction, which he has never had. Age-related degeneration is the most common cause.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.q: A 50-year-old woman with chronic lung disease and a low oxygen saturation feels her heart skipping. Her tracing shows that every other beat (bigeminy) is early, wide and bizarre, with no P wave before it. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Early, wide and bizarre QRS complexes with no P wave are premature ventricular contractions, here every other beat (bigeminy); hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes.
Premature junctional contractions are early and narrow, with an inverted, hidden or trailing P wave; her early beats are wide and bizarre.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ventricular tachycardia is three or more consecutive premature ventricular beats; she has single wide beats alternating with normal ones.
Premature atrial contractions are early but narrow, with an abnormally shaped P wave in front; her early beats are wide with no P wave.

B.q: A 70-year-old man with a 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is scheduled for elective repair. He asks how the surgeon will choose between endovascular and open repair. Which factor guides the choice?
opts: Correct. Two methods exist, endovascular aneurysm repair with a modular graft placed through the iliac or femoral arteries, and open replacement with a tube or bifurcated graft; the choice considers age and medical comorbidities.
Whether he has a carotid bruit
A carotid bruit relates to carotid disease, not the aortic repair method. The choice between endovascular and open repair rests on age and comorbidities.
Skin color has no bearing on the repair method. The surgeon weighs the patient's age and medical comorbidities in choosing endovascular or open repair.
The result of his ankle index
The ankle-brachial index grades leg arterial disease and does not choose the aneurysm repair. Age and comorbidities decide between endovascular and open.

B.q: The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group of endocarditis organisms comes from which source?
opts: The genitourinary tract is the source of enterococci, not the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms, which come from the upper respiratory tract.
The gastrointestinal tract is the source of Streptococcus gallolyticus. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group comes from the upper respiratory tract.
The skin is the source of staphylococci. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract.
Correct. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract.

B.q: In a stable narrow complex tachycardia, which step comes before any drug?
opts: Imaging does not terminate the rhythm; in a stable narrow complex tachycardia the first step is a vagal maneuver.
Intravenous procainamide is used for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White and is not a first step; stable narrow complex tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.
Correct. A vagal maneuver is first line for stable supraventricular (narrow complex) tachycardia, before adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability.
Synchronized cardioversion is immediate treatment only when the patient is unstable; a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.

B.q: Which is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II block?
opts: Catheter ablation destroys tissue and is itself a named cause of Mobitz type II. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent, temporary measure that bridges the patient to definitive therapy, which is a permanent pacemaker.
Correct. The definitive treatment for Mobitz type II block is a permanent pacemaker, because the block can progress unpredictably to complete heart block and sudden death.
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator shocks lethal ventricular rhythms. A failing conduction system needs a permanent pacemaker instead.

B.q: A 37-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 4 weeks ago and now feels well. A repeat electrocardiogram shows widespread T-wave inversions without ST elevation, and troponin is normal. Which best explains the tracing?
opts: Correct. The classic evolution is widespread ST elevation with PR depression, then ST normalization with T-wave flattening, then inversion of the flattened T waves, and finally a normal tracing.
Tamponade gives low voltage and electrical alternans with hemodynamic signs, not isolated T-wave inversion in a well patient.
With normal troponin and a known recent pericarditis, diffuse T-wave inversion fits the third stage of the pericarditis evolution.
ruled out by a stated finding
Hyperkalemia peaks the T waves rather than inverting them; this is the expected evolution of pericarditis.

B.q: A 12-year-old had a ventricular septal defect closed with a prosthetic patch 4 months ago and is now scheduled for a dental extraction. Which is the most appropriate step regarding endocarditis?
opts: Correct. The first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device is a high-risk period, and extraction manipulates the gums, so prophylaxis is given.
Within 6 months of repair with prosthetic material, the child is high risk and prophylaxis is indicated.
ruled out by a stated finding
Prophylaxis is given before the procedure so the drug is circulating during the bacteremia.
Delay is not the recommendation; a prophylactic dose before the extraction is, during the 6-month high-risk window.

B.q: A 73-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidosis. She has right-sided heart failure and asks how her condition compares with other kinds of heart muscle disease. Which statement about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Complete recovery in most patients is the course of stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis of all heart muscle diseases.
Poorest of all heart muscle diseases
Correct. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis among all types of heart muscle disease, and it often presents at an advanced stage with pronounced cardiopulmonary symptoms.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy carries the poorest prognosis among heart muscle diseases rather than a better one, partly because it presents late.
A normal life span with diuretics
Diuretics relieve congestion but do not change the outlook, which is the poorest among heart muscle diseases. Transplantation is an option in advanced disease.

C.q: A 58-year-old man with chest pain develops a wide tachycardia whose QRS shape varies from beat to beat; his QT interval was normal earlier. He is defibrillated and returns to sinus rhythm. Which study is the most urgent next?
opts: Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia without a long QT is most often from acute ischemia, so after defibrillation it needs urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.
Ambulatory monitoring confirms whether symptoms match intermittent bradycardia; an ischemic polymorphic tachycardia needs urgent coronary angiography.
The stroke-risk score guides anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation; after polymorphic ventricular tachycardia from ischemia the priority is coronary angiography.
Digoxin toxicity is a listed cause of junctional rhythm and of block; polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with chest pain and a normal QT points to ischemia.

C.q: An 80-year-old man has an incidental finding on a preoperative electrocardiogram: a constant PR interval in conducted beats with occasional P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex, and no PR lengthening before the dropped beats. He has no symptoms. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the tracing in a year
Waiting ignores the unpredictable progression of Mobitz type II to complete heart block and sudden death. A pacemaker is indicated.
Reassurance suits silent first-degree or Mobitz type I block. Mobitz type II needs a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms.
A beta blocker slows atrioventricular conduction and could worsen the block. Mobitz type II is treated with a permanent pacemaker.

Correct. Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms, because of unpredictable progression to complete block and a poor prognosis, so the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

C.q: A 29-year-old woman has had a resting heart rate of 110 to 120 for months, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and a drug screen are normal, and she takes no medications or stimulants. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes, at an atrial rate of 250 or more; she has one normal P wave per beat.
Focal atrial tachycardia has one abnormally shaped P wave from an ectopic focus and typically starts abruptly; her P waves are normal sinus P waves.
Correct. A sinus tachycardia that stays unexplained after secondary causes have been excluded is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, a diagnosis of exclusion with a usually benign prognosis.
Appropriate sinus tachycardia is a response to physiologic stress, illness or a drug; every such cause has been looked for and excluded here.

C.q: A 48-year-old woman is discharged on ibuprofen and colchicine for acute pericarditis. Which new symptom should prompt her to go straight to the emergency department rather than call for an appointment?
opts: Mild fatigue in the late afternoon
Mild fatigue is common during recovery and is not a red flag. Lightheadedness with breathlessness suggests low cardiac output.
Mild indigestion after doses of ibuprofen
Indigestion is a medication side effect to discuss and protect against; it is not a red flag for tamponade.

Correct. Red-flag symptoms for tamponade or worsening disease, such as dyspnea, lightheadedness or falling exercise tolerance from low cardiac output, need emergency evaluation rather than a routine visit.
Pain that still eases on leaning forward
Persistent positional pain needs follow-up but is the expected pattern; hemodynamic symptoms are the emergency red flags.

C.q: A 76-year-old woman is brought in after fainting twice today. She is pale, with a blood pressure of 84/50, and her lead II rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: Correct. P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR, then a P wave with no QRS, is Mobitz type II block; with fainting and hypotension the emergent treatment is transcutaneous pacing, followed by a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine is used to slow or stop a regular supraventricular tachycardia, a fast rhythm; this slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes needs pacing.
A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II block, but with fainting and hypotension right now she first needs emergent transcutaneous pacing.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia with a pulse; this is a slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes, which needs pacing.

C.q: Why can a positive D-dimer not confirm deep vein thrombosis?
opts: A negative result is reassuring, since the test is sensitive. The problem is that a positive result is nonspecific.
Correct. A positive D-dimer means fibrinolysis is occurring somewhere in the body, which many conditions cause, so imaging is needed to show a clot in the leg veins.
D-dimer is a blood test and cannot show a location. It cannot confirm a clot because many conditions raise it.
D-dimer marks fibrin breakdown in any vascular bed. It cannot confirm a venous clot because many conditions raise it.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: How is the diagnosis of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy confirmed?
opts: ST elevation and T wave inversion look like acute coronary syndrome; they do not confirm the diagnosis. Catheterization does.
Troponin is usually elevated but is not specific; it cannot separate stress cardiomyopathy from an infarct. Catheterization confirms it.
Biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not the confirmatory test here, which is catheterization showing normal coronaries.
Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed by cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries despite the wall-motion abnormality and elevated troponin.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. C.q: A 61-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis develops worsening breathlessness, crackles and a new loud regurgitant murmur on day 3 of appropriate antibiotics. Echocardiography shows a ruptured chord with severe regurgitation. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery, and cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for surgery.
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs; it does not address valve failure.
Palliative care may join a multidisciplinary plan, but heart failure from valve dysfunction calls for surgical evaluation.
This is a hospital problem needing urgent surgical evaluation, not an outpatient visit.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
C.q: An 8-year-old with endocarditis has a sudden fulminant illness with high spiking fevers, unlike the usual slow course in children. Which organisms does this presentation suggest?
opts: Fungal disease is tied to neonatal central lines; fulminant fevers suggest pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.
Viridans streptococci cause the usual indolent pediatric course, not a fulminant one.
Correct. A fulminant presentation with high spiking fevers suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus, while most children have an indolent course.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci are tied to prosthetic material and lines, not fulminant spiking fevers.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
C.q: An 81-year-old man reports dizziness and two fainting spells. His pulse is 36, and his rhythm strip is shown, with arrows marking R waves and P waves. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS
A constant PR with occasional dropped beats is Mobitz type II block; on this strip the distance from P wave to QRS changes every beat.
P waves and QRS complexes at unrelated rates

Correct. The P waves march at their own regular rate and the slow QRS complexes at another, with no fixed relation: complete dissociation of the atria from the ventricles, third-degree (complete) block, ventricular rate usually under 40.
PR lengthens until a QRS is dropped
Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped QRS is Mobitz type I block; here the P waves keep no consistent relation to the QRS at all.
Every P wave conducted with a long PR
A long, constant PR with every P wave conducted is first-degree block; here most P waves are not followed by a QRS, and the two run at different rates.
C.alt: Rhythm strip with regularly spaced P waves (upward arrows) and slower complexes (downward arrows) that fall at varying distances from the P waves

C.q: A 47-year-old woman has a tender, red, firm segment along a forearm vein after a peripheral intravenous catheter was removed. Venous duplex ultrasound shows a superficial vein with a thickened wall. Which additional finding would establish thrombophlebitis rather than phlebitis alone?
opts: Correct. Wall thickening alone is phlebitis, inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus. Thickening together with clot in the lumen is thrombophlebitis, and the distinction matters because treatment differs.
Wall thickening is already present and is common to both phlebitis and thrombophlebitis. Only clot within the lumen turns the picture into thrombophlebitis.
A perivenous fluid collection would raise concern for abscess or infection around the vein. Thrombophlebitis is defined by clot within the lumen of the thickened vein.
Valve reflux belongs to chronic venous disease such as varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency. It says nothing about clot inside an inflamed superficial vein.

C.q: A 57-year-old woman whose QT interval became prolonged after starting a new medication has palpitations, and the monitor shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline (torsades de pointes). She is awake, and intravenous magnesium has been given. If an antiarrhythmic is added, which one can be used?
opts: Procainamide is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT; it is used instead for pre-excited atrial fibrillation and stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.
Beta blockers such as metoprolol are avoided in torsades de pointes because the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly the QT.

Correct. In torsades de pointes magnesium is the treatment, and intravenous lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used (with little evidence), because amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT and beta blockers lengthen it indirectly.
Amiodarone is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT further; lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used.

C.q: A 64-year-old man with crushing chest pain develops a wide QRS tachycardia whose complexes vary in shape from beat to beat; his QT before the episode was normal. He is still talking and has a pulse. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state, so it is defibrillated even when the patient has a pulse and looks well.
Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS; it suits unstable monomorphic rhythm. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated.
Watching is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never stable and is defibrillated.
Drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia needs defibrillation.

C.q: A 75-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve needs a dental extraction. He had a mild delayed rash (no hives, swelling or anaphylaxis) with penicillin and cannot take oral medication. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Penicillin-allergic patients unable to take oral medication receive cefazolin or ceftriaxone intramuscularly or intravenously, provided there is no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.
Ampicillin is a penicillin; the injectable penicillin is for patients without penicillin allergy.
ruled out by a stated finding
Azithromycin is an oral option, and he cannot take oral medication; cefazolin or ceftriaxone by injection fits.
ruled out by a stated finding
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

C.q: A 21-year-old man collapses while playing basketball and arrives with a very fast regular tachycardia. He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70. A vagal maneuver fails, and adenosine slows the rate to reveal an irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, each with a delta wave (slurred upstroke). Which is the next step?
opts: More adenosine blocks only the normal node, leaving the accessory pathway free to conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.
Atropine speeds conduction and treats unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster.

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is never repeated: nodal blockade leaves the accessory pathway unopposed.
An oral beta blocker is too slow and, as a nodal blocker, leaves the accessory pathway unopposed; procainamide is the drug used.

C.q: Which is the first treatment for torsades de pointes in a conscious patient?
opts: Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided in torsades because the slower rate lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.
Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades, followed by more magnesium as an infusion.

C.q: A 71-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an exacerbation and respiratory failure. His pulse is 128 and irregular. The electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every QRS, with at least three different P-wave shapes in lead II. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Flutter shows uniform sawtooth waves at 250 or more; his discrete P waves in three different shapes point to multifocal atrial tachycardia.

Correct. An irregular tachycardia with a P wave for every QRS and at least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, usually from severe lung disease or heart failure in an acutely ill patient.
Focal atrial tachycardia is regular, with one consistent abnormal P wave from a single focus, not three shapes.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves at all; his rhythm has a P wave before every QRS, in three shapes.
ruled out by a stated finding

C.q: A 73-year-old man with ischemic rest pain notices that walking around the room eases his foot pain, although walking used to cause calf pain. Which explanation should he be given?
opts: Rest pain is not relieved by a pain-relief response; it resists even narcotics. Standing and walking help because dependency lets gravity assist arterial flow.
Dependency uses gravity to aid flow
Correct. Rest pain is relieved by hanging the leg over the bed or walking around, a paradox: unlike claudication, walking uses the gravity effect of dependency on extremity perfusion.
Lower pressure would reduce perfusion, not improve it. The relief comes from dependency, where gravity aids arterial flow to the forefoot.
Venous drainage is not the reason. Standing and walking put the foot in a dependent position, and gravity then helps perfuse it.

C.q: A 29-year-old man returns from a camping trip in Connecticut with fatigue and an expanding red rash around a tick bite on his thigh. His electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.30 seconds with every P wave conducted. Which infection should be suspected as the cause of his conduction delay?
opts: Endocarditis causes block through an abscess near the conduction system, usually with fever and a murmur. A tick bite with an expanding rash points to Lyme disease.
Chagas disease causes complete block in people from areas where it is endemic. A tick bite in New England with an expanding rash points to Lyme disease.
A sore-throat virus is not a named cause of atrioventricular block. The tick bite and rash point to Lyme carditis.
Correct. Lyme disease (Lyme carditis) is a named infectious cause of atrioventricular block at every degree, and a tick bite with an expanding rash points to it.

C.q: Which finding makes outpatient therapy for deep vein thrombosis inappropriate?
opts: Good support and reliable follow-up favor outpatient treatment. An iliofemoral proximal clot makes it inappropriate.
Correct. Outpatient therapy is not appropriate for iliofemoral proximal clots, concurrent symptomatic pulmonary embolism, high bleeding risk or comorbidities needing inpatient care.
Hemodynamic stability favors outpatient treatment. An iliofemoral proximal clot makes it inappropriate.
Absence of renal insufficiency favors outpatient treatment. An iliofemoral proximal clot makes it inappropriate.

C.q: Which feature belongs to acute rather than subacute infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Acute infective endocarditis rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites; subacute disease rarely metastasizes.
Rarely metastasizing is a feature of subacute endocarditis. The acute form seeds extracardiac sites.
Slow structural damage, if any, belongs to subacute endocarditis. Acute disease rapidly damages cardiac structures.
An indolent course is the subacute form. Acute endocarditis is hectically febrile and seeds distant sites.

C.q: A 41-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated for tricuspid valve endocarditis. On day 2 he develops a new cough, and chest imaging shows several new scattered lesions in both lungs. Which complication best explains these findings?
opts: Correct. The lung is among the listed embolic complications of infective endocarditis, and septic pulmonary infarcts count as a vascular phenomenon under the modified Duke criteria.
Heart failure from valve dysfunction floods the lungs diffusely; it does not make scattered lesions. Septic emboli to the lung do.
Antibiotic lung toxicity is not the listed complication; the lung is an embolic site of endocarditis, and septic pulmonary infarcts are a vascular phenomenon.
Aspiration causes a dependent pneumonia, not scattered lesions in both lungs; septic pulmonary emboli are a listed embolic complication.

C.q: A 38-year-old man who drinks several energy drinks a day is told his skipped beats are premature ventricular contractions. Which description best fits these beats?
opts: Early, wide and bizarre, with no P wave
Correct. A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles, so the early beat has a wide (over 0.12 seconds), bizarre QRS and no P wave; caffeine and stimulants are among the triggers.
Early and narrow, with an inverted P wave
An early narrow beat with an inverted P wave in II, III and aVF is a premature junctional contraction; a ventricular beat is wide and bizarre.
Early and narrow, with an abnormal P wave
An early narrow beat with an abnormally shaped P wave is a premature atrial contraction; a ventricular beat is wide with no P wave.
Wide, with a slurred upstroke and short PR
A short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) on every beat is pre-excitation; a premature ventricular beat is early with no P wave at all.

C.q: A 72-year-old woman with tamponade from a newly found effusion and no known cancer is being evaluated. Which consideration about the cause is most important at her age?
opts: Her age makes the cause irrelevant
The cause drives long-term prognosis and management; at her age malignancy deserves particular attention.
Correct. Older adults with an effusion or tamponade warrant a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, while younger patients are more often idiopathic or viral.
Dressler syndrome follows myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery, which she has not had.
Coxsackievirus is a classic viral cause, usually after a viral illness. At her age, with tamponade and no known cause, malignancy should be suspected more strongly.

C.q: A 34-year-old man has occasional premature junctional contractions (early narrow beats with no visible P wave) on a monitor and is anxious about them. He has no symptoms and no heart disease. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Catheter ablation has no role in occasional, benign premature junctional beats that cause no symptoms.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms from block or sinus failure, not occasional early beats.
A beta blocker such as metoprolol is for persistent symptoms or frequent beats; he has neither.
Correct. No treatment is needed if premature junctional contractions are asymptomatic and infrequent, and reassurance of the benign nature of the rhythm is often adequate.

C.q: A 66-year-old man who had cardiac surgery last year reports palpitations and fatigue. His blood pressure is normal, and his rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Repeating sawtooth (flutter) waves outnumber the narrow QRS complexes because the atrioventricular node blocks some of them: atrial flutter, common after atrial scarring from cardiac surgery.
Sinus tachycardia has one upright P wave before each QRS at 100 to 160; this strip has several identical atrial waves for every QRS, the sawtooth of flutter.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no organized atrial waves; this strip shows regular, repeating sawtooth waves between the QRS complexes.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia has one P wave per QRS in at least three shapes; here several identical sawtooth waves fall between each pair of QRS complexes.
C.alt: Rhythm strip of narrow complexes with a continuous zigzag baseline of identical small waves between them, two to four per complex

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 46-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 20 years has six months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). The apical impulse is displaced laterally and a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25%, and coronary angiography shows no significant narrowing. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy is a transient regional weakness of the mid and apical segments after a stressor, mostly in postmenopausal women, not a slow global dilation over months.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows a thick, often asymmetric septum with a small cavity and a normal or high ejection fraction, not thin, dilated walls with an ejection fraction of 25%.

Correct. Dilation and impaired contraction without severe coronary disease or pressure or volume overload define dilated cardiomyopathy, and long-term excess alcohol is one of its named causes. The displaced apical impulse and third heart sound fit a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy keeps a near-normal cavity size and systolic function with stiff walls and big atria. Dilated, thin walls with poor squeeze are the dilated pattern instead.

C.q: A 52-year-old man with a pacemaker implanted two weeks ago has three days of swelling and aching of the left arm. The pacemaker lead has injured the wall of the subclavian vein. Which component of the Virchow triad does this injury represent?
opts: A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency from inherited disorders, cancer, estrogen or pregnancy. Mechanical injury to the vein wall from a lead is endothelial trauma instead.

Correct. Damage to the vessel lining from an indwelling device is endothelial trauma, one leg of the Virchow triad. Pacemakers, implanted defibrillators and central venous catheters are the most common causes of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis.
Impaired lymphatic drainage causes lymphedema and is not part of the Virchow triad. Injury to the subclavian vein wall is endothelial trauma, the third triad component.
Venous stasis arises from immobilization, heart failure or venous insufficiency. A lead scraping the vein wall is physical injury to the lining, which is the endothelial trauma component.

C.q: A 67-year-old woman with suspected restrictive cardiomyopathy has right-sided heart failure and big atria on echocardiogram. Her cardiologist wants to measure pressures inside both ventricles to characterize the filling problem. Which invasive test evaluates ventricular pressure tracings?
opts: Correct. Cardiac catheterization is useful in restrictive cardiomyopathy to evaluate ventricular pressure tracings, alongside cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and, when needed, endomyocardial biopsy.
Exercise echocardiography assesses functional capacity and obstruction, mainly in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Ventricular pressure tracings need catheterization.
Transesophageal echocardiography images the valves and chambers with ultrasound but does not record direct ventricular pressure tracings. Cardiac catheterization does.
Biopsy samples tissue to confirm or exclude a diagnosis; it does not record pressure tracings. Catheterization measures ventricular pressures.

C.q: Which acute limb ischemia categories leave time for vascular imaging?
opts: Imaging time shrinks as the category worsens. Only viable and marginally threatened limbs have time for it.
Immediately threatened limbs need prompt revascularization in a surgical suite. Viable and marginally threatened limbs allow imaging.
Irreversible limbs usually need no imaging because amputation is required. The viable and marginally threatened limbs allow it.
Correct. Viable and marginally threatened limbs have sufficient time for vascular imaging such as computed tomography angiography; immediately threatened limbs go to a surgical suite.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman in urgent care has a fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages (dark lines under the nail plates). Before transfer, a colleague proposes giving a dose of ceftriaxone right away. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites are exactly what she needs before any antibiotic.
Echocardiography is part of the workup, looking for vegetations; it should not be avoided.
Correct. Empiric therapy is started only after blood cultures have been drawn; antibiotics given first may sterilize the cultures and lose the organism.
Endocarditis is managed in hospital with parenteral antibiotics and close monitoring, so admission is appropriate.

C.q: A 70-year-old woman has a 1.4 cm femoral pseudoaneurysm on ultrasound after cardiac catheterization. She is comfortable and the limb is well perfused. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Open surgery is not the listed treatment for a small pseudoaneurysm. Under 2 cm, it may thrombose and regress on its own with watchful waiting.
Heparin anticoagulates and would work against the thrombosis that seals a pseudoaneurysm. Under 2 cm the plan is to watch and wait.
Thrombolysis dissolves clot in acute limb ischemia. A small pseudoaneurysm is expected to seal by clotting, so it is watched.
Correct. A pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm in diameter may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression, so watchful waiting is appropriate.

C.q: A 59-year-old man is about to start hemodialysis through a newly created forearm arteriovenous fistula. Which self-check should he be taught to confirm that the fistula is working?
opts: Confirm it stays full when raised
A healthy fistula collapses completely when the arm is elevated. An access that stays distended on elevation is not behaving normally.
Confirm the skin over it is cool
Skin temperature is not how function is judged, and a cool arm suggests poor perfusion. A working fistula is checked by the thrill and soft bruit.
Confirm no sound is heard over it
A healthy fistula makes a soft bruit heard with a stethoscope, with systolic and diastolic components. Silence over the access is a warning sign.
Correct. A healthy fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit, so he can feel the buzzing over the access. Loss of the thrill signals a problem and should be reported promptly.

C.q: Which set lists the four rhythms that produce cardiac arrest?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation, atrial fibrillation, complete heart block and torsades with a pulse
Atrial fibrillation and complete heart block usually keep a pulse. The four arrest rhythms are ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity and asystole.
Pulseless electrical activity, bigeminy, first-degree block and sinus tachycardia

Bigeminy, first-degree block and sinus tachycardia all produce a pulse. The four arrest rhythms are ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity and asystole.
Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity, asystole
Correct. Cardiac arrest results from ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity or ventricular standstill (asystole).
Asystole, sinus bradycardia, Mobitz type II block and atrial flutter with rapid response

Sinus bradycardia, Mobitz type II and atrial flutter are perfusing rhythms. The arrest rhythms are ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity and asystole.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
C.q: A 68-year-old man who smokes and has diabetes reports aching in both buttocks and hips after walking two blocks, relieved by about 10 minutes of rest. He also reports erectile dysfunction. Both femoral pulses are diminished. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Buttock and hip claudication points to the aortoiliac segment, and the triad of claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction is Leriche syndrome, the severe form of aortoiliac disease.
Tibial and peroneal disease produces foot claudication with normal femoral pulses. Buttock pain, erectile dysfunction and weak femoral pulses point to the aortoiliac segment.
Spinal stenosis mimics claudication but brings numbness and weakness and is relieved only by sitting or leaning forward. It does not diminish the femoral pulses or cause this triad.
Superficial femoral stenosis gives upper two-thirds calf claudication, the most common site. Buttock and hip pain with weak femoral pulses places the lesion higher, in the aortoiliac segment.

C.q: A 71-year-old man has palpitations, chest pressure and crackles at both lung bases. His pulse is irregularly irregular at 170 with no P waves on the monitor, and his blood pressure is 76/48. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Adenosine treats regular supraventricular tachycardia; an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves is atrial fibrillation, and he is unstable.
Intravenous rate control is for atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate in a hemodynamically stable patient; his hypotension and pulmonary edema call for a shock.
Outpatient cardioversion after 21 days of anticoagulation suits stable atrial fibrillation; an unstable patient needs synchronized cardioversion now.
Correct. Atrial fibrillation with hypotension and pulmonary edema is a hemodynamically unstable medical emergency, and unstable atrial fibrillation is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

C.q: A 40-year-old woman has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 182 with palpitations and mild anxiety. Her blood pressure is 128/80, oxygen saturation 98%, and she is alert without chest pain. Which treatment should be tried first?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is reserved for the unstable patient; she is stable, so a vagal maneuver comes first.
Adenosine comes second, after a vagal maneuver fails, in stable supraventricular tachycardia.
Amiodarone is tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not as the first step in a stable narrow complex tachycardia.
Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine (up to twice), keeping synchronized cardioversion for instability.

C.q: A 24-year-old man collapses during a basketball game and wakes within a minute. In the ambulance his rhythm is irregular, with wide QRS complexes of varying width at rates approaching 300. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia is the other wide-complex tachycardia, but it is regular at about 150 to 200; this rhythm is irregular and approaches 300.
Atrial flutter with 2:1 block is regular with narrow QRS complexes and sawtooth waves; this rhythm is irregular and wide.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but narrow, with three or more P-wave shapes, in acutely ill lung patients; this rhythm is wide and near 300.

Correct. An irregular, wide-complex rhythm with rates approaching 300 is atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway (with Wolff-Parkinson-White); ventricular tachycardia is regular at 150 to 200.

C.q: A 44-year-old man had a tuberculous pericardial effusion drained in the hospital and is starting antituberculous therapy. Which specialty should be part of his close follow-up?
opts: Correct. Close clinical follow-up is tailored to the underlying etiology: cardiology, infectious disease, nephrology, oncology or rheumatology; a tuberculous effusion calls for infectious disease.
Nephrology follows a uremic effusion in kidney failure. A tuberculous effusion on antituberculous therapy is followed closely with infectious disease.
Medical oncology follows a malignant effusion. A tuberculous effusion on antituberculous therapy is followed closely with infectious disease.
Rheumatology follows an autoimmune effusion such as lupus. His tuberculous effusion is followed by infectious disease, which guides antituberculous therapy.

C.q: A 66-year-old man had coronary bypass surgery two months ago. He now has palpitations and fatigue. His heart rate is 150 and regular, and the electrocardiogram shows sawtooth waves, two for every narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has a normal P wave before each QRS, not two sawtooth waves per QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Sawtooth flutter waves with two for every narrow QRS are atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the most common ratio, and atrial scarring after surgery is a classic setting.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no organized atrial waves; his rhythm is regular with sawtooth waves.
ruled out by a stated finding
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three or more distinct P-wave shapes, not uniform sawtooth waves.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 35-year-old woman has 3 days of sharp substernal chest pain that improves when she sits forward. Her vital signs are normal, and no rub is heard on careful auscultation. Which additional finding would complete the clinical diagnosis of acute pericarditis?
opts: B-type natriuretic peptide is not among the four criteria (chest pain, friction rub, electrocardiogram changes, effusion); widespread ST elevation would complete the diagnosis.
Pericardial calcification on a radiograph is not one of the four criteria; widespread ST elevation on the electrocardiogram would complete the diagnosis.

Correct. The diagnosis needs two of four criteria: sharp substernal chest pain, a friction rub, suggestive electrocardiogram changes (widespread ST elevation) and a new or worsening effusion. Her pain plus the electrocardiogram would make two.
A troponin above the reference range
Troponin is not a diagnostic criterion; an elevated value would suggest myocardial involvement (myopericarditis) and higher risk.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: A 59-year-old man with a large pericardial effusion from metastatic cancer reports a hoarse voice, hiccups and difficulty swallowing. Which mechanism explains his hoarseness?
opts: The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue and is far from the pericardium. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is impinged.
Direct invasion of the vocal cords
The effusion does not invade the larynx. It compresses the recurrent laryngeal nerve on its course through the chest.
Vena cava obstruction swells the face and arms; hoarseness comes from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Correct. Large effusions can cause dysphagia, nausea, hiccups, cough and hoarseness, the hoarseness from impingement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

C.q: A 49-year-old woman has subacute endocarditis, and her blood cultures grow Eikenella corrodens, a member of the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms; gram-negative Eikenella and its group are treated with ceftriaxone.
Correct. HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone, or ampicillin-sulbactam.
Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not the treatment for these gram-negative organisms.
Rifampin is an add-on for staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, not therapy for Eikenella, which is ceftriaxone.

C.q: A 64-year-old woman with hypertension has a carotid bruit found on routine examination. She has never had neurologic symptoms. Duplex shows 35% stenosis. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Stenting is an alternative revascularization for poor surgical candidates who meet surgical thresholds. A 35% asymptomatic stenosis needs medical management.

Correct. Medical management is advised for symptomatic and asymptomatic patients with low-grade stenosis under 50%: antiplatelet therapy, control of hypertension, diabetes and lipids, smoking cessation, diet, exercise and weight reduction.
Endarterectomy is reserved for symptomatic stenosis over 70% or asymptomatic stenosis over 80% with a life expectancy over five years. A 35% stenosis is managed medically.
Digital subtraction angiography is used to guide interventions, and none is indicated here. Low-grade stenosis under 50% is managed medically.

C.q: A 44-year-old man develops a first calf deep vein thrombosis one week after minor knee arthroscopy under a local nerve block, followed by a long car trip. Which duration of anticoagulation is appropriate?
opts: Three months is for a major transient risk factor such as surgery under general anesthesia, prolonged hospitalization or major trauma. His minor surgery and travel are minor factors, warranting three to six months.

Correct. A clot provoked by a minor transient risk factor, such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery, prolonged travel or minor leg injury, is treated for three to six months, chosen from the patient's history.
Indefinite treatment is reserved for an unprovoked first clot. His clot has identifiable transient triggers, so open-ended anticoagulation is not needed.
Six weeks is below the three-month minimum that applies to every first venous thromboembolism. His clot warrants three to six months.

C.q: A 70-year-old man has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and malaise that began a week after a dental extraction. A new murmur of mitral regurgitation is heard. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn. Which organism are they most likely to grow?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus is a skin organism that causes acute, toxic disease; a smoldering course after dental work points to viridans streptococci.
Candida causes fungal endocarditis in the immunocompromised and in patients with central lines, not subacute disease after a tooth extraction.
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract, not the mouth; an oral source after dental work brings viridans streptococci.
Correct. The oral cavity is the source of viridans streptococci, the classic cause of subacute endocarditis after dental procedures and the organism dental prophylaxis targets.

opts: Splinter hemorrhages are nail-bed signs of endocarditis and do not affect conduction. An abscess is the cause of the block.
Increased vagal tone causes milder nodal blocks. Complete block during endocarditis points to an abscess.
Correct. Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is a named cause of complete heart block, because the infection extends into the conduction tissue.
Septic pulmonary emboli cause cough and lung lesions, not heart block. An abscess near the conduction system does.

C.q: A 52-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency and recurrent ulcers is being considered for an invasive venous procedure. Which test is the gold standard for defining his venous anatomy beforehand?
opts: This measures arterial pressure to exclude peripheral artery disease before compression. It says nothing about venous anatomy, which catheter venography defines.
Correct. Catheter-based venography is the gold standard, rarely needed to make the diagnosis, and is performed before an invasive intervention to define the anatomy.
Duplex is the first test to confirm the diagnosis, rule out clot and find reflux. It is noninvasive and not the gold standard used before an intervention.

C.q: In tachy-brady syndrome, which tachyarrhythmia is most common?
opts: In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation, not a sinus tachycardia.
Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome a tachyarrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or with offset pauses.
Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm, but it is not the usual tachyarrhythmia of tachy-brady syndrome; atrial fibrillation is.

C.q: A 20-year-old man with acute myocarditis after a flulike illness is on the ward with heart failure symptoms. He reports new palpitations, and his nurse notes a brief episode of lightheadedness. Which complication poses the most immediate threat to his life?
opts: Pericardial thickening marks constrictive pericarditis, the differential of restrictive cardiomyopathy. Myocarditis threatens life through ventricular arrhythmia.
Mitral valve prolapse is a valve disorder unrelated to myocarditis. Palpitations with near-syncope in myocarditis signal ventricular arrhythmia or heart block.
Aortic dissection is not a complication of myocarditis. The life-threatening risk behind palpitations and presyncope here is ventricular arrhythmia or heart block.

Correct. Palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death in myocarditis are due to underlying ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block, and myocarditis can cause rapidly progressive, often fatal, arrhythmia.

C.q: A 59-year-old man has frequent premature atrial contractions on a monitor (early beats with abnormal P waves), many per minute. He has no known heart disease. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
opts: An accessory pathway is suspected with a short PR and delta wave; frequent premature atrial beats prompt a structural workup.
Correct. If premature atrial contractions are frequent, look for underlying structural heart disease; in a diseased heart they may precede supraventricular tachycardia, fibrillation or flutter.
Digoxin toxicity is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, not of frequent premature atrial beats; frequent premature atrial contractions prompt a search for structural heart disease.
Infrequent, asymptomatic beats need nothing, but frequent ones prompt a search for structural heart disease.

C.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy. His father had a cardiomyopathy and his older brother died suddenly at 35. No alcohol, drug or chemotherapy exposure is found. Which is the most appropriate referral for him and his family?
opts: Biopsy is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy and is not a family screening tool. The step for a positive family history is genetic counseling.
Most dilated cardiomyopathy presents between 20 and 60, and his brother died at 35. Waiting until 60 would come too late; genetic counseling is indicated now.
Reassurance that it is not inherited
A family history of cardiomyopathy and sudden death is a red flag for familial disease, which is common and usually autosomal dominant. Reassurance would miss relatives at risk.

Correct. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy accounts for up to 35% of cases, usually autosomal dominant, and genetic counseling is part of patient education when there is a family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death.

C.q: A 70-year-old man presents with painful blue toes and palpable pedal pulses. On abdominal examination there is a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus. Which lesion is the likely source of his emboli?
opts: A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows catheterization and causes local pain from swelling. A pulsatile abdominal mass with blue toes indicates an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Dissection presents with sudden tearing chest pain from an intimal tear. The pulsatile abdominal mass here is an abdominal aortic aneurysm shedding emboli to the toes.
Correct. Atheroemboli originate from proximal atherosclerotic plaques, and an abdominal aortic aneurysm can itself shed emboli, producing blue toe syndrome as one of its embolic phenomena.
Carotid plaque embolizes to the brain, causing transient ischemic attack or stroke. Emboli to the toes with a pulsatile abdominal mass come from the aorta.

opts: Amiodarone is for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. Premature beats are addressed by finding and correcting hypoxemia or electrolytes.
Ablation is reserved for refractory symptoms or beat-induced cardiomyopathy. The first step is to correct hypoxemia and electrolytes.
Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes of premature ventricular contractions, so new frequent beats call for checking oxygenation and electrolytes first.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. He has isolated premature beats with a pulse.

C.q: A 76-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and diabetes has two spells of lightheadedness this week. Her electrocardiogram shows regular P waves, a constant PR interval of 0.16 seconds in the conducted beats, and occasional P waves with no QRS complex after them, with no lengthening of the PR beforehand. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: In complete block no P wave conducts and the P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated. Here most P waves conduct at a fixed PR.
Correct. A constant PR interval with random dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz type II block; acquired His-Purkinje disease from age, hypertension and diabetes is its most common cause.
First-degree block has a long PR and never drops a beat. Here the PR is normal and some P waves fail to conduct.
Mobitz type I lengthens the PR before each dropped beat. Here the PR stays constant, which marks Mobitz type II.

C.q: Which imaging test is now recommended for risk stratification of complicated or recurrent pericarditis?
opts: Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance is recommended for risk stratification of complicated or recurrent pericarditis; edema or late gadolinium enhancement shows active inflammation.
Coronary angiography assesses the coronary arteries; with right heart catheterization it occasionally confirms constriction, but it does not stratify recurrent pericarditis.
A chest radiograph is typically normal in pericarditis and cannot show active inflammation. Cardiac magnetic resonance can.
A ventilation-perfusion scan looks for pulmonary embolism and has no role in stratifying pericarditis. Cardiac magnetic resonance does.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
C.q: Constriction that persists after a coexisting pericardial effusion has been drained defines which entity?
opts: Subacute tamponade is fluid under pressure that builds more slowly; draining it relieves the compression. Persistent constriction after drainage marks effusive-constrictive disease.
Recurrent pericarditis is a return of symptoms after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks. Constriction that outlasts drainage of an effusion is effusive-constrictive pericarditis.
Correct. Effusive-constrictive pericarditis combines underlying constriction with a coexisting effusion, usually with tamponade, and the constriction persists after the effusion is drained.
A loculated posterior effusion is a pocket of fluid that cannot be reached percutaneously and may need a window. It does not leave constriction behind once drained.
