C.q: A 45-year-old woman has a catheter-related deep vein thrombosis of the right arm and asks how likely a pulmonary embolism is compared with a leg clot. Which statement is accurate?
opts: About 3% for arm and leg clots alike

About 3% is the estimated fatal-embolism rate for untreated symptomatic non-massive pulmonary embolism, not the frequency of embolism, which differs by site: up to 6% for arm and 15% to 30% for leg clots.
15 to 30%, versus up to 6% for leg clots
This reverses the figures. Pulmonary embolism complicates 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots and only up to 6% of upper-extremity clots, so her risk is the lower one.
Under 1% for arm clots, 6% for leg clots
Under 1% is the untreated fatal-embolism estimate for a clot without pulmonary embolism. The actual frequency of embolism is up to 6% for arm clots and 15% to 30% for leg clots.
Up to 6%, versus 15 to 30% for leg clots
Correct. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper-extremity deep vein thromboses, versus 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots. Arm clots are only 5% to 10% of all deep vein thromboses.

C.q: A 68-year-old man who smoked for 40 years has no symptoms, but a widened, pulsatile aorta is felt on routine abdominal examination. Which is the study of choice for initial screening for an aneurysm?
opts: A plain film shows a calcified outline in only about 75% of aneurysms and misses the 25% that are not calcified. Ultrasound is the screening study of choice.
Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study. The initial screening study for an aneurysm is abdominal ultrasound.
Correct. Abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic study of choice for initial screening for the presence of an aneurysm and is also used for serial documentation of aneurysm size.
Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without dye or radiation and suits stable patients with dye allergy. Screening starts with ultrasound.

C.q: Which combination of modified Duke criteria establishes definite infective endocarditis?
opts: One major plus one minor criterion makes endocarditis possible, not definite; three minor would be needed.
Three minor criteria make endocarditis possible. Definite needs five minor, one major and three minor, or two major.
Correct. Definite endocarditis is documented by two major criteria, one major and three minor criteria, or five minor criteria.
Two minor criteria alone reach neither definite nor possible; possible needs three minor or one major plus one minor.

C.q: A 27-year-old man admitted with presumed viral myocarditis keeps deteriorating despite full medical treatment. Coronary angiography is normal, and valvular, toxic and ischemic causes of heart failure have been excluded. Which test establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Catheterization and angiography are used to rule out coronary ischemia as the cause of new heart failure, and his were normal. Biopsy is what establishes myocarditis.

Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis once other causes of heart failure are excluded, and it is recommended for acute deterioration of unknown origin that does not respond to treatment.
The chest radiograph in myocarditis is nonspecific and may only show cardiomegaly. The gold standard is endomyocardial biopsy.
Troponin indicates myonecrosis but does not identify its cause. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard that establishes myocarditis.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
C.q: When is hospice referral appropriate in cardiomyopathy?
opts: Adolescent care centers on genetic screening and activity restriction for high risk. Hospice referral is for end-stage disease.
Correct. Palliative care covers symptom management, advance care planning, goals-of-care discussions and caregiver support, with hospice referral in end-stage cardiomyopathy.
A first arrhythmia calls for treatment and risk review, not hospice. Hospice referral is reserved for end-stage cardiomyopathy.
Sodium restriction is routine adult lifestyle care. Hospice referral is appropriate in end-stage cardiomyopathy.

C.q: A 69-year-old man has long-standing constrictive pericarditis with marked edema and ascites despite diuretics. A computed tomography scan shows a thick, heavily calcified pericardium. Which treatment offers definitive relief?
opts: Correct. Constrictive pericarditis is often a surgical disease; pericardiectomy, removal of part or most of the pericardium, is the definitive treatment and gives a 5-year survival near 80%.
Pericardiocentesis drains fluid and is the definitive treatment for tamponade. A thick, calcified pericardium must be removed surgically.
The myocardium is not the problem in constriction. Removing the scarred pericardium is the definitive treatment.
Anti-inflammatory therapy suits early, stable constriction; established calcified disease needs pericardiectomy.

C.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia?
opts: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not a drug to speed a slow heart; atropine is first line.
Correct. Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine slows conduction through the atrioventricular node and is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia; it would worsen a bradycardia.
A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acute, unstable patient first gets atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.

C.q: A 34-year-old woman has visible, dilated, tortuous veins of the thigh and calf that are tender to palpation, with aching heaviness after prolonged standing. Which is the most common predisposing factor for her condition?
opts: Correct. The most common predisposing factor for varicose veins is family history, so ask whether relatives have them, and how old they were when they developed.
Heavy lifting produces periods of high venous pressure and adds risk. It is less common than family history, the leading predisposing factor for this condition.
Women are at higher risk after pregnancy, and it is a recognized risk factor. Family history remains the most common predisposing factor for varicose veins.
Long periods of standing raise venous pressure and are a recognized risk factor. It is not the most common predisposing factor, which is family history.

C.q: A 41-year-old man with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes to the emergency department with exertional chest pressure. His electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy without acute changes, and a clinician reaches for a chest pain order set. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Amiodarone is used in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death and to control atrial fibrillation. It is not the drug to avoid.

Correct. Drugs that reduce preload or afterload, such as nitrates, may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so nitroglycerin should be avoided if possible in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Metoprolol, a beta blocker, is the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction and improves diastolic filling. It is used, not avoided.
Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used to treat outflow tract obstruction. The drug to avoid is a nitrate such as nitroglycerin.

C.q: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia and severe hypoxia becomes unresponsive. No pulse can be felt, yet the monitor shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 80 with a P wave before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: The tracing looks like normal sinus rhythm, but there is no pulse and no perfusion, which makes it pulseless electrical activity, a cardiac arrest.
ruled out by a stated finding
Asystole is a flat line with no P waves and no QRS complexes; this monitor shows an organized rhythm, which without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no QRS complexes; this monitor shows regular, narrow complexes with P waves.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An organized rhythm you would expect to produce a pulse, with no perfusing beats, is pulseless electrical activity, not asystole; hypoxia and hypovolemia are its two leading causes in adults.

C.q: A 47-year-old woman 5 days after hip surgery has sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a heart rate of 118. Her new electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.14 seconds with an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection) in V1 to V3. Which underlying problem best explains the new conduction finding?
opts: Valvular heart disease, especially aortic stenosis, is a listed cause of left bundle branch block; her rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is a right bundle branch block.
Lyme carditis is a listed cause of atrioventricular block, such as first-degree, Mobitz and complete block; a sudden right bundle branch block after surgery fits pulmonary embolism.

Correct. A wide QRS with an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is right bundle branch block, and a sudden increase in right ventricular pressure from pulmonary embolism is a listed cause, the one that fits a sudden new block in this setting.
An accessory pathway produces a short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), not an rsR' pattern; her new right bundle branch block fits pulmonary embolism.

C.q: At what age does aortic dissection usually occur outside Marfan syndrome?
opts: Correct. Aortic dissection usually occurs in the 60s and 70s, except in Marfan syndrome, with males more affected than females and hypertension present in most cases.
Young onset fits Marfan syndrome, the stated exception. Otherwise dissection occurs in the 60s and 70s.
That is older than the stated range. The typical age for aortic dissection is the 60s to 70s.
That is younger than the stated range. Dissection usually occurs in the 60s and 70s.

C.q: A 65-year-old woman has new atrial fibrillation at 146 with palpitations. She is alert, her blood pressure is 132/84, and she has no chest pain or breathlessness. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response gets intravenous rate control; rate control is the first goal.
Synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.
Mapping and ablation is a later, elective rhythm option, not the first treatment of rapid ventricular response.
Atropine speeds the heart and is for unstable bradycardia; it would worsen rapid ventricular response.

D.q: A 63-year-old woman whose hypotension was relieved by pericardiocentesis for a malignant effusion asks about her outlook. Which statement best describes her prognosis?
opts: The drained volume does not set long-term prognosis; the underlying cause, here cancer, does.
Drainage has cured her for good
Drainage relieves the acute event, but malignant effusions often recur, and the cancer sets the long-term outlook.
The underlying cancer will drive it

Correct. For cardiac tamponade the short-term outcome is often good with prompt treatment, but long-term prognosis depends on the underlying cause; a symptomatic malignant effusion has a median survival of 2 to 4 months.
A viral effusion usually passes; a malignant one carries a limited life expectancy and frequent recurrence.

D.q: A 71-year-old man hospitalized for six days with pneumonia develops swelling of the left calf. His team considers using the Wells criteria to estimate his probability of deep vein thrombosis. Which statement about applying the Wells criteria to him is accurate?
opts: A low score replaces all testing
A low score does not replace testing; it leads to a D-dimer first, and only a negative result stops the work-up. The score guides which test comes next, not whether to test.
Meant for outpatient or emergency use

Correct. The Wells criteria are used in the outpatient and emergency department settings, not for inpatients, in whom the score is less useful. A hospitalized patient needs clinical judgment and ultrasound rather than this pathway.
The score is less useful in hospitalized patients; it is validated for outpatients and emergency department patients. Inpatients need clinical judgment and ultrasound instead of this pathway.
The Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis address suspected leg clots, with items such as calf swelling and pitting edema of the leg. Upper-extremity clots are not what this score was built for.

D.q: A 74-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness. Her office electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 64, but her family has noticed a slow pulse during the spells. Which is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
opts: Urgent coronary angiography follows defibrillation of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia from ischemia; intermittent slow spells need ambulatory monitoring first.
A permanent pacemaker is for symptomatic bradycardia once symptoms are shown to correlate with it; that correlation has not yet been confirmed.

Correct. In suspected sick sinus syndrome the key step is to confirm whether symptoms correlate with episodes of bradycardia, as a 24-hour ambulatory recording does; with correlation a pacemaker follows, without it observation is appropriate.
Observation is appropriate only if symptoms turn out not to match bradycardia; that has to be established by monitoring before she is reassured.

D.q: An 84-year-old woman spent 9 days in the hospital for a large pericardial effusion that needed two procedures. She is now weak and needs help to walk. Besides cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, which service is most appropriate before she goes home?
opts: Correct. Older adults are more likely to need rehabilitation after prolonged illness and procedures, which also carry higher morbidity and mortality at her age.
Genetic evaluation is not indicated for her pericardial disease. She needs rehabilitation.
Infectious disease follows an infectious cause such as tuberculosis, which nothing here suggests. Rehabilitation after her prolonged illness is the need.
Nephrology joins the follow-up when uremia causes the effusion, which nothing here suggests. Rehabilitation addresses her weakness and deconditioning.

opts: Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Symptomatic first-degree block with a PR over 0.3 seconds is managed with a pacemaker.
Correct. First-degree block causes symptoms once the PR interval exceeds 0.3 seconds, and a permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic patients when no reversible cause is found.
Cardioversion terminates tachycardias. A long PR interval with a normal rate is a conduction delay, which is paced, not shocked.
Reassurance fits the asymptomatic patient. Symptoms with a PR above 0.3 seconds make him a candidate for a permanent pacemaker.

D.q: A 72-year-old woman has ischemic rest pain and a nonhealing toe ulcer, with an ankle-brachial index of 0.3. Angiography shows a long femoral-popliteal occlusion. Which treatment is principally used for her degree of disease?
opts: Correct. A bypass graft, using a saphenous vein or synthetic graft around the diseased segment, is principally used to treat severe critical leg ischemia and is highly effective.
Exercise therapy improves walking distance in claudication. Rest pain with tissue loss is critical limb ischemia, which is principally treated with a bypass graft.
Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative given for claudication symptoms. It cannot rescue a limb with rest pain and an ulcer; bypass grafting is the principal treatment.
Intravenous heparin is for acute peripheral arterial occlusion. Chronic critical limb ischemia with a long occlusion is principally treated with a bypass graft.

D.q: What does gadolinium add to magnetic resonance imaging in suspected myocarditis?
opts: Imaging cannot culture a virus. Gadolinium improves visibility of inflammation and its extent.
Troponin is a blood test for myonecrosis. Gadolinium imaging shows the extent of inflammation.
Excluding coronary ischemia is the role of cardiac angiography, not gadolinium magnetic resonance imaging.
Correct. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging improves visibility and shows the extent of myocardial inflammation.

D.q: A 70-year-old woman has Mobitz type II block found on a routine tracing; she has no symptoms. Her family prefers to avoid procedures. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II, so it should not be avoided; observation alone should be.
Referral is appropriate for a pacemaker evaluation. The approach to avoid is simple observation of Mobitz type II.

Correct. Observation alone should be avoided because Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms; its progression is unpredictable, so the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Checking for drugs that slow conduction is reasonable and not harmful. What should be avoided is observation without a pacemaker.

D.q: A 26-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is leaving for a summer hiking trip in a hot climate. She takes a beta blocker and asks how to lower her risk of symptoms while away. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should maintain hydration, because dehydration lowers preload and worsens outflow obstruction; diuretics are used with caution for the same reason.
Restrict fluids to soften the murmur
Fluid restriction reduces preload, which worsens obstruction and makes the murmur louder. Education is to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration.
Use alcohol to relax at the campsite
Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are taught to avoid excess alcohol consumption, alongside keeping well hydrated and avoiding competitive exertion.
Take extra diuretic on hot days
Diuretics lower preload and can aggravate outflow obstruction; they are used with caution to avoid dehydration. Extra doses in the heat would be dangerous.

D.q: An 80-year-old man is brought in dizzy and confused, with a blood pressure of 78/44. His electrocardiogram shows P waves at 76 and wide QRS complexes at 32, with no relationship between them. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for complete block, but a confused, hypotensive patient needs emergent transcutaneous pacing first.

Correct. Atria and ventricles beating at separate rates is third-degree (complete) block; with confusion and hypotension the emergent treatment is transcutaneous pacing, and the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Amiodarone treats ventricular tachycardia, a fast wide rhythm; a slow escape rhythm at 32 from complete block needs transcutaneous pacing.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; this is a slow escape rhythm at 32 from complete block, which needs pacing.

D.q: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure is admitted with a tender, swollen left calf, and duplex ultrasound confirms deep vein thrombosis. Her daughter asks why heart failure raises the risk of a clot. Which Virchow triad component should the clinician name?
opts: An elevated platelet count is not one of the three Virchow triad components. Heart failure raises clotting risk through slowed venous flow, which is venous stasis.

A hypercoagulable state comes from inherited thrombophilia, cancer, estrogen therapy or pregnancy. Heart failure raises clot risk by slowing venous return, which is stasis rather than a change in clotting chemistry.
Correct. Heart failure is listed under venous stasis, the Virchow component reflecting altered blood flow. A weak pump lets blood pool and slow in the veins of the legs, so clots form more readily.
Endothelial trauma is injury to the vein wall from surgery, fracture, burns or injection. Heart failure does not damage the vessel lining; it reduces venous flow, the stasis component.

D.q: A 19-year-old woman with a week of fever and myalgia now has severe breathlessness. She is cold and clammy with a blood pressure of 78/50, heart rate 128, raised jugular venous pressure and crackles throughout both lungs. Myocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Biopsy can establish the diagnosis later, but it is not done before a patient in shock is stabilized. Aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first.

Correct. Myocarditis can present as cardiogenic shock, and although supportive care is the mainstay, treatment is directed toward the scenario and may require aggressive hemodynamic stabilization first.
She is in cardiogenic shock, a presentation of myocarditis that can be rapidly fatal. Delay is unsafe; aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first.
Exercise testing has no place in cardiogenic shock. Myocarditis this severe needs aggressive hemodynamic stabilization.

D.q: An 81-year-old man has known tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) and asks which fast rhythm is behind his palpitations. An ambulatory monitor is arranged. Which rhythm is it most likely to record during the fast episodes?
opts: Flutter is an organized atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; it is not the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome the tachyarrhythmia that alternates with bradycardia or pauses is most commonly atrial fibrillation.
A junctional rhythm is slow and regular, usually 40 to 60, not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Ventricular tachycardia can occur in some patients, who then need a defibrillator with the pacemaker, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.

D.q: A 63-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve is having a tooth extracted tomorrow. He has no drug allergies and takes pills without difficulty. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. A high-risk patient (prosthetic valve) having an extraction gets a single dose of oral amoxicillin 30-60 minutes before the procedure, targeting viridans streptococci.
A prosthetic valve is a high-risk condition, and extraction manipulates gums and roots, so prophylaxis is indicated.
ruled out by a stated finding
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
Prophylaxis is a single dose given before the procedure, not a week of antibiotics afterward.

D.q: A 58-year-old woman has a slow sinus rhythm at 38 six hours after an inferior myocardial infarction. She feels faint and her blood pressure is 80/50. Each narrow QRS has a normal P wave before it. Which drug should be given first?
opts: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, a listed cause of sinus bradycardia; it would slow her further.
Diltiazem is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, another drug cause of bradycardia; it would worsen her hypotension and slow rate.
Adenosine stops supraventricular tachycardia by blocking the atrioventricular node; it has no place in an unstable bradycardia.
Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia, here from an infarction affecting the conduction tissue, is treated first with atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.

D.q: A 69-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has a preoperative 12-lead electrocardiogram, which is shown. The QRS lasts 0.16 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia is a regular wide rhythm at 100 to 250; this tracing has wide complexes at a normal rate, from slowed conduction in one bundle.
Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave); this pattern of deep V1 complexes and broad lateral R waves is a bundle branch block.
Right bundle branch block gives an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL; here V1 to V3 are deep and downward.

Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with a deep, dominant S wave in V1 and broad, upright lateral complexes without Q waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block; chronic hypertension is a common cause.
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram with wide complexes, deep downward complexes in V1 to V3 and broad upright complexes in the lateral leads

D.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes is told his new palpitations come from atrial fibrillation. Which description best fits his electrocardiogram?
opts: Irregular, with three or more P-wave shapes
Irregular beats with three or more P-wave shapes are multifocal atrial tachycardia; atrial fibrillation has no P waves to count.
Regular, with a P wave before each beat
A regular rhythm with a P wave before each beat is a sinus rhythm; atrial fibrillation has no P waves and no regularity.
Irregularly irregular, with no P waves
Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval; the QRS is narrow, and the rate is often 110 to 160 but can be under 80 or over 200.
Regular, with sawtooth waves between beats
Regular sawtooth waves describe atrial flutter, in which the node conducts a fixed share of the waves; atrial fibrillation has no organized atrial activity.

D.q: A 71-year-old man's asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measured 4.1 cm six months ago and now measures 4.8 cm. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: That interval is for a stable 4.0 to 5.4 cm aneurysm. Rapid growth of more than 0.5 cm in six months is itself an indication for repair.
Three-yearly surveillance is for stable 3.0 to 3.9 cm aneurysms. Growth of 0.7 cm in six months is rapid and calls for repair.
Correct. Evidence of rapid growth, 0.5 cm in six months, is an indication for repair regardless of size; his aneurysm grew 0.7 cm, and fast expansion also raises rupture risk.
Size is only one trigger; rapid expansion of 0.5 cm in six months is another. His 0.7 cm growth means repair now, not waiting.

D.q: A 59-year-old man is on day 6 of antibiotics for aortic valve endocarditis. He still has fevers, and today's electrocardiogram shows a new conduction block not present on admission. Which complication best explains the new conduction abnormality?
opts: Chordal rupture causes a new regurgitant murmur and heart failure, not a conduction block.
Correct. When infection extends beyond the leaflets into the myocardium as a perivalvular abscess and reaches the upper ventricular septum, it interrupts the conduction system.
Extension into the epicardium causes pericarditis. Conduction block follows extension into the upper ventricular septum.
Septic emboli lodge in organs such as the lung, spleen and kidney; they do not explain a new conduction block, which points to a septal abscess.

D.q: A 72-year-old woman has 6 weeks of aching and stiffness in her shoulders and hips, fatigue and a low-grade fever. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are high, but no murmur is heard and three sets of blood cultures are negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Polymyalgia rheumatica sits in the differential of endocarditis because it causes myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers, but there is no murmur and cultures are negative.
Atrial myxoma would give fever with a new murmur, such as a tumor plop; she has no murmur.
ruled out by a stated finding
Antiphospholipid syndrome mimics endocarditis through thromboemboli and valve disease, not girdle myalgia.
Subacute endocarditis brings a new murmur and positive cultures in most patients; neither is present here.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.q: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and an acute dissection has had his systolic pressure lowered to 110 mmHg and his pain controlled. Which definitive treatment removes the diseased segment?
opts: Endarterectomy removes carotid plaque. A dissected aorta is repaired by grafting and replacing the diseased portion.
Correct. Beyond blood pressure reduction and pain management, surgery grafts and replaces the diseased portion of the aorta in aortic dissection.
Thrombolysis dissolves arterial clot in acute limb ischemia. Dissection is definitively treated by grafting and replacing the diseased aorta.
Thrombin injection seals a pseudoaneurysm leak. Dissection needs surgical grafting and replacement of the diseased aorta.

D.q: A 24-year-old marathon runner has an electrocardiogram at a sports physical. He has no symptoms. The PR interval grows longer with each beat until one P wave is not followed by a QRS complex, and then the cycle repeats. The QRS complexes are narrow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mobitz type II drops beats without warning while the PR interval stays constant. Here the PR lengthens before each drop.
Correct. A PR interval that progressively lengthens until a QRS drops, in a repeating pattern, is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block; increased vagal tone is a named cause in well-conditioned people.
First-degree block has a long but constant PR and never drops a beat. Here a P wave fails to conduct after the PR lengthens.
Complete block has no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. Here the PR changes in an orderly pattern tied to the drop.

D.q: A 70-year-old man who had a large anterior myocardial infarction three weeks ago develops sudden pain and coldness of his right leg with absent foot pulses. Which cardiac finding is the most likely embolic source?
opts: Valve calcification is not the named cardiac source. After a myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus is the classic origin of an embolus to the leg.
Fluid around the heart does not form emboli. The cardiac sources named for limb emboli are atrial fibrillation and left ventricular thrombus after infarction.

Correct. Thromboemboli are the most common emboli, and the heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases; a left ventricular thrombus after myocardial infarction is a named example, as is atrial fibrillation.
A septal scar is not a recognized embolic source here. Following myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus can dislodge and occlude a smaller distal artery.

D.q: A 64-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy has breathlessness on exertion and peripheral edema. On examination her neck veins distend when firm pressure is held over her right upper abdomen, a sign called hepatojugular reflux (neck-vein distension with firm pressure over the liver). Which additional finding is expected with this degree of congestion?
opts: A pulsatile mass in the epigastrium
A pulsatile abdominal mass suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm, not venous congestion. With hepatojugular reflux the expected finding is congestive hepatomegaly.
Flank ecchymosis signals retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm. Venous congestion from a failing heart gives hepatomegaly and ascites instead.
Correct. The gastrointestinal findings of dilated cardiomyopathy are congestive hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux and ascites, all from venous congestion as the failing heart backs up blood.
Venous congestion enlarges the liver rather than shrinking it. Congestive hepatomegaly sits with hepatojugular reflux and ascites in the dilated cardiomyopathy examination.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 62-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 2 years ago has 3 weeks of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Her blood pressure is 128/80 without hypotension. The chest radiograph shows an enlarged, water-bottle (globular) cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Which test is required to confirm a pericardial effusion?
opts: Angiography images the coronary arteries, not the pericardial space. Echocardiography confirms an effusion.
A radiograph suggested the effusion with a globular silhouette but cannot confirm it. Echocardiography is required.
Correct. Clinical evaluation, electrocardiogram and chest radiograph may suggest a pericardial effusion, but an echocardiogram is required to confirm it and to assess its hemodynamic significance.
Low voltage may hint at fluid, but the electrocardiogram cannot confirm an effusion. Echocardiography can.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 35-year-old man who recently moved from a region where tuberculosis is common has effusive pericarditis. Pericardial fluid is positive on acid-fast stain. Which treatment may significantly reduce his progression to constriction?
opts: Aspirin treats inflammation, not the mycobacterial infection driving the scarring. Antituberculous therapy does.
Correct. If tuberculosis is the underlying etiology, treatment of the tuberculosis may significantly reduce progression to constrictive pericarditis.
Pericardiectomy treats established constriction; treating the tuberculosis is what reduces progression to it.
Diuretics relieve fluid overload but leave the infection untreated. Antituberculous therapy reduces progression.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 58-year-old woman received mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy for a chest cancer 15 years ago. She now has progressive exercise intolerance, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), ascites and swollen legs. Echocardiogram shows stiff ventricles of normal size, marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function with a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Myocarditis follows a recent viral prodrome with acute heart failure and raised troponin. A slow course years after radiation with stiff ventricles is restrictive disease.
Chemotherapy can also cause dilated cardiomyopathy, but that gives dilated, thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction. Stiff, normal-sized ventricles with big atria are restrictive.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited, with an asymmetric thick septum and outflow murmur. Treatment-related fibrosis with big atria is restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Correct. Mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy cause inflammation and then fibrosis that restricts filling, and a prior history of radiation or chemotherapy is a named clue in restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. D.q: A 61-year-old man with a long QT has recurrent runs of torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline). Between runs he is alert, with a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which is the first treatment?
opts: Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Magnesium is the first treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided because the slower rate indirectly lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium comes first.
Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades, followed by more magnesium as an infusion.

D.q: Which causes should be checked first in a patient with frequent premature ventricular contractions?
opts: High cholesterol and obesity are coronary risk factors, not the named causes to check. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium) are the causes to look for first.
Hypertension and diabetes drive degenerative conduction disease. Premature ventricular contractions come mainly from hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance.
Dehydration and fever are not the named causes. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances head the list for premature ventricular contractions.

Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) are the main causes, so new frequent premature ventricular contractions call for checking oxygen and electrolytes.

D.q: Where are patients with Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy admitted?
opts: No surgical treatment applies. Patients are admitted to cardiology and managed as acute coronary syndrome at first.
Correct. Because the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome with no reliable early differences, patients follow acute coronary syndrome protocols and are admitted to cardiology.
Discharge is unsafe when the syndrome cannot be told from acute coronary syndrome early. Patients are admitted to cardiology.
The trigger is often emotional, but the condition is a cardiac syndrome that mimics acute coronary syndrome; admission is to cardiology.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for ventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
D.q: An 82-year-old woman has an electrocardiogram at a routine visit and has no symptoms. The rhythm is regular at 70, every P wave is followed by a narrow QRS, and the PR interval is a constant 0.26 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A constant PR interval over 0.20 seconds with every P wave conducted is first-degree atrioventricular block; the vast majority cause no symptoms, and age-related degeneration of the conduction system is the most common cause.
Mobitz type II has a constant PR with randomly dropped QRS complexes; every one of her P waves is followed by a QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding
Mobitz type I lengthens the PR progressively until a QRS is dropped; her PR is long but constant, and every P wave is conducted.
ruled out by a stated finding
Third-degree block shows P waves with no association to the QRS complexes and a ventricular rate usually under 40; she conducts every P wave at 70.

D.q: How is hemodynamically stable atrial flutter treated first?
opts: Ablation is the definitive management of flutter, chosen for recurrence rather than as the first step; a stable patient starts with rate control using a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Adenosine is used for supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; the stable patient starts with rate control.
Correct. Stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; an unstable patient gets synchronized cardioversion.

D.q: A 52-year-old man has an electrocardiogram before a dental procedure. Among normal sinus beats at 74 is an occasional early, narrow QRS preceded by a P wave that is inverted in II, III and aVF, with a PR interval under 0.12 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A premature ventricular contraction is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave; this early beat is narrow and carries an inverted P wave.
ruled out by a stated finding
A premature atrial contraction has an early, abnormally shaped P wave from the atria, but an inverted P in II, III and aVF with a short PR marks a junctional origin.
Wolff-Parkinson-White gives a short PR on every sinus beat, with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave); here only the occasional early beat differs.
Correct. An early, narrow QRS whose P wave is inverted in II, III and aVF with a short PR comes from the atrioventricular junction: a premature junctional contraction, usually without symptoms.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. D.q: From which point is the typical 4-6 week course of antibiotics for infective endocarditis counted?
opts: Correct. Therapy runs typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture, so persistently positive cultures push the start of the clock later.
Counting from the first positive culture would shorten treatment for patients whose bacteremia persists. The clock starts at the first negative culture.
Defervescence is not the marker. The course is counted from the first negative blood culture.
Admission day is not the anchor. The 4-6 weeks run from the first negative blood culture.

D.q: A 26-year-old man has a sudden, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 230 with retrograde (inverted) P waves. An electrocardiogram taken last year in normal sinus rhythm showed a short PR interval and a delta wave (a slurred QRS upstroke). Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Sinus tachycardia runs from just above 100 up to 160 with a P wave before every QRS; a rate of 230 with retrograde P waves is a reentrant rhythm.
ruled out by a stated finding
Nodal reentry is a circuit within the atrioventricular node, usually at 140 to 180, and it does not explain the short PR interval and delta wave on his sinus tracing.
Atrial fibrillation is the irregular supraventricular tachycardia; his rhythm is regular, and the earlier pre-excitation points to an accessory pathway.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Pre-excitation (a short PR interval and a delta wave) on an earlier tracing in normal sinus rhythm points to an accessory pathway and the potential for atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia, which runs above 100, usually at 200 to 300, with hidden or retrograde P waves.

D.q: What is the first-line treatment for stable supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia; a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.
Adenosine is second, given if a vagal maneuver fails in stable supraventricular tachycardia, and it may be repeated once.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, where adenosine must be avoided; stable supraventricular tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.
Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine (which may be repeated once); an unstable patient gets immediate synchronized cardioversion.

D.q: A 61-year-old woman with heart failure has palpitations. A 48-hour monitor shows several runs of 4 to 8 identical wide QRS beats, each lasting a few seconds, without hemodynamic compromise. Which is the first-line drug?
opts: Correct. Symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is treated first with a beta blocker such as metoprolol or carvedilol.
Adenosine is used in narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia gets a beta blocker first.
Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia starts with a beta blocker.
Digoxin is not named for ventricular tachycardia. A beta blocker is the first-line drug.

D.q: A 26-year-old healthy man has an incidental right bundle branch block on a pre-employment electrocardiogram. His examination and echocardiogram are normal, and he asks whether this means he has heart disease. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: It proves a past heart attack
A right bundle branch block does not prove an old infarction. It may occur with no apparent underlying heart disease.
Isolated right bundle branch block does not inevitably progress to complete block. It may occur with no apparent heart disease.
An isolated right bundle branch block does not need pacing; treatment depends on the underlying condition.
It can occur without heart disease
Correct. A new right bundle branch block is not always pathological; it may occur in people with no apparent underlying heart disease, and treatment depends on any underlying condition.

D.q: A 29-year-old woman has had a resting heart rate of 105 to 115 for a year. Thyroid tests, a blood count, a drug screen and an echocardiogram are normal, and she takes no medications or stimulants. Her electrocardiogram shows a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more; she has a normal P wave before each QRS at a rate near 110.
Nodal reentry is a paroxysmal, regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves; hers is a persistent sinus rhythm with visible normal P waves.
Correct. A sinus tachycardia that remains unexplained after secondary causes are excluded is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, a diagnosis of exclusion.
Focal atrial tachycardia has an abnormally shaped P wave from an ectopic focus and starts abruptly; her P waves are normal sinus P waves.

D.q: What does the word part "athero" in atherosclerosis refer to?
opts: The clot at a site of rupture
Thrombosis at a rupture site is a later event in the plaque sequence. Athero, gruel or paste, refers to the fatty material in the plaque's core.
The fibrous cap over the plaque
The fibrous tissue forming over the plaque is what the sclerosis half (hardness) describes. Athero, gruel or paste, names the fatty core beneath it.
The fatty core of the plaque
Correct. Athero means gruel or paste and refers to the fatty material in the core of the plaque; sclerosis (hardness) refers to the fibrous tissue that stiffens the wall over it.
The calcium in the arterial media
Medial calcific sclerosis is a separate form of arteriosclerosis. Athero, meaning gruel or paste, names the fatty material in the plaque's core.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 63-year-old man with a peripherally inserted central catheter for chemotherapy develops a tender cord in the upper arm. Venous duplex ultrasound shows extensive clot burden in a superficial vein. He has active cancer and a prior deep vein thrombosis. Which therapy should be added to compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug?
opts: Correct. With extensive clot burden or an intermediate or higher risk of thrombosis, anticoagulation may be started, using unfractionated heparin, low molecular weight heparin such as enoxaparin, or fondaparinux.
Corticosteroids do not treat clot and can worsen thrombotic risk. When clot burden is extensive or thrombotic risk is higher, the added therapy is a heparin or fondaparinux.
Aspirin is not among the agents given for this problem. The listed options for extensive clot or higher thrombotic risk are unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin and fondaparinux.
Antibiotics are for infection within the vein, suggested by high fever, purulence or redness beyond the vein. This bland extensive clot in a high-risk patient calls for anticoagulation.

D.q: A 66-year-old woman in torsades de pointes (a polymorphic rhythm whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline) becomes unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/30 and only a faint pulse. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A polymorphic rhythm has no consistent QRS to synchronize to. Unstable torsades is defibrillated.
Pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms with a pulse. Unstable torsades needs defibrillation.
Correct. A hemodynamically unstable patient in torsades de pointes is defibrillated (unsynchronized cardioversion); polymorphic rhythms are not synchronized.
Lidocaine may be used in the stable patient. Instability calls for defibrillation.

D.q: A 66-year-old man has long-standing pitting edema of the lower leg with brown pigmentation and a healed medial ankle ulcer. Duplex ultrasound shows thickened, scarred valve leaflets and chronic obstruction of the femoral vein. He does not recall any leg clot. Which is the most likely cause of his condition?
opts: Correct. Scarred valve leaflets with chronic proximal obstruction are post-thrombotic changes, and prior deep vein thrombosis is the leading cause even though about a quarter of patients recall no clot.
Superficial reflux is another common cause, but it produces dilated veins with incompetent valves. Thickened, scarred leaflets with obstruction point to an earlier clot.
A pelvic tumor can obstruct venous outflow, but it does not scar the valve leaflets of the leg veins. Post-thrombotic valve scarring points to an earlier deep vein thrombosis.
A fistula is a rare cause that produces venous hypertension by shunting arterial blood. Scarred valves and femoral vein obstruction are the signature of a prior clot.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 33-year-old woman eight weeks postpartum has mild calf aching and a low pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis. Her clinician orders a D-dimer. Which characteristic makes a negative result useful for excluding a clot?
opts: D-dimer is a blood test that detects fibrin breakdown and cannot show a clot. Visualizing the thrombus is the job of venous duplex ultrasound.
D-dimer is not specific; many conditions raise it, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot. Its value as a rule-out test comes from high sensitivity.
Testing whether a vein compresses is done with duplex ultrasound, not a blood test. D-dimer rules out disease through its sensitivity, not through any imaging feature.

Correct. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so a negative result in a low-likelihood patient effectively rules out deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It cannot confirm a clot, since fibrinolysis has many causes.

D.q: A 70-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has three months of progressive hoarseness. A chest radiograph shows widening of the mediastinal shadow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A descending aneurysm compresses the trachea or esophagus, giving dyspnea, stridor, cough or dysphagia. Hoarseness points to the arch.
Correct. Thoracic aneurysm symptoms depend on location: an arch aneurysm causes hoarseness by involving the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and the chest film shows a widened mediastinum.
An ascending aneurysm causes aortic regurgitation and heart failure rather than hoarseness. Hoarseness localizes the aneurysm to the arch.
An abdominal aneurysm causes abdominal, back or flank pain and cannot involve the recurrent laryngeal nerve or widen the mediastinum.

D.q: A 66-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction wears a 24-hour monitor. It shows several runs of 5 to 8 consecutive wide, identical beats at 150, each lasting under 10 seconds and stopping on its own. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sustained ventricular tachycardia lasts 30 seconds or more or causes collapse sooner; his runs end on their own in under 10 seconds.
Premature atrial contractions are single early narrow beats with abnormal P waves; his runs are wide, consecutive and ventricular.

Correct. Three or more consecutive premature ventricular beats is ventricular tachycardia, and runs lasting under 30 seconds are nonsustained; identical QRS shapes make it monomorphic, which is common with heart disease such as prior infarction.
Ventricular fibrillation is uncoordinated activity with no pulse and no perfusion; his runs are organized, identical wide beats that stop on their own.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. D.q: Which is the most common site of infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Infective endocarditis most commonly affects the heart valves, which is why a new murmur from valve damage is such an important finding.
Infection can sit on the low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect, but this is far less common than infection of the heart valves.
Intracardiac devices are a recognized site and a growing predisposing condition, but the heart valves remain the most common site of infection.
The pericardial sac is the site of pericarditis, not endocarditis. Infective endocarditis most commonly involves the heart valves.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. D.q: A 23-year-old competitive cyclist has a regular rhythm at 50 with narrow QRS complexes and no visible P waves on a screening electrocardiogram. He has no symptoms, and his echocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Training explains his high vagal tone and is not harmful here; he needs no treatment.
Correct. A junctional rhythm can be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as well-conditioned athletes, and needs no treatment when asymptomatic in an otherwise healthy person.
Atropine is for acute, unstable, symptomatic bradycardia; he is an asymptomatic, healthy athlete.
A pacemaker is for junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome, not an asymptomatic athlete.

D.q: A 22-year-old man has sudden palpitations and lightheadedness. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 112/70. His 12-lead electrocardiogram is shown. Which drug is the most appropriate?
opts: Intravenous rate control suits ordinary atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate; an irregular, wide rhythm through an accessory pathway is treated with procainamide.

Correct. A very fast, irregular rhythm with wide complexes of changing width is atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway (pre-excited atrial fibrillation); intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine.
When atrial fibrillation runs with Wolff-Parkinson-White, adenosine must not be used; the drug for pre-excited atrial fibrillation is intravenous procainamide.
Lidocaine is a choice for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, which is regular at about 150 to 200; this wide rhythm is irregular and approaches 300.
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram of a very rapid, irregular rhythm with wide complexes whose width and height vary from beat to beat

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 62-year-old man collapses in a hospital hallway. He is unresponsive with no pulse, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is started. His monitor strip is shown. Which is the most important next step?
opts: Correct. Chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS complexes and no pulse is ventricular fibrillation, treated as cardiac arrest with defibrillation (an unsynchronized shock) as soon as possible, then 2 minutes of compressions.
Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent treatment for unstable bradycardia from high-grade block; this pulseless chaotic rhythm needs defibrillation.
Amiodarone is added for ventricular fibrillation that persists after shocks and epinephrine; the first priority in this arrest is an immediate unsynchronized shock.
Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a QRS complex, so it is for a tachycardia with a pulse; ventricular fibrillation has no QRS to time to and needs defibrillation.
D.alt: Rhythm strip of continuous, irregular, low-to-medium waves with no recognizable P waves or complexes

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for venous disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
D.q: Advancing age raises deep vein thrombosis risk above which age?
opts: Thirty is far younger than the age flagged. Deep vein thrombosis risk is listed as increased above 60 years, alongside obesity, smoking and heart failure.
Fifty is not the threshold given for deep vein thrombosis. Risk is listed as increased above 60 years.
Correct. Age over 60 years is listed among the other risk factors for deep vein thrombosis, alongside obesity, smoking, heart failure and a personal or family history of clot.
Seventy-five is later than the flagged age. Deep vein thrombosis risk is listed as increased above 60 years, well before this.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 64-year-old man has restrictive cardiomyopathy confirmed on imaging, but cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and genetic testing have not identified a cause. His team is considering endomyocardial biopsy. When is biopsy performed in this condition?
opts: When imaging and genetic tests are negative

Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is performed when all imaging studies and genetic testing are negative, or when a tissue sample is likely to confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management.
As the first test in every suspected case
Biopsy is not the first test; echocardiography, electrocardiogram and radiograph come first, then cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Biopsy follows negative imaging and genetic testing.
Never, since it cannot change management
Biopsy is performed precisely when a tissue sample could confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management, after negative imaging and genetic tests.
Only after cardiac transplantation is done
Biopsy is used during the diagnostic work-up, when imaging and genetic testing are negative, not only after transplantation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 58-year-old woman with acute endocarditis asks why the team is so worried when she felt well a week ago. Which statement about untreated acute endocarditis is accurate?
opts: It is mainly a lung infection
Acute disease damages the valves and seeds many extracardiac sites; lung emboli are only one of them.
Smoldering for months is the subacute form; acute disease is rapidly destructive.
Acute endocarditis does not resolve on its own; untreated, it progresses to death within weeks.
It can be fatal within weeks
Correct. Acute endocarditis rapidly damages cardiac structures and seeds extracardiac sites; if untreated, it progresses to death within weeks.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 28-year-old man had a cold 10 days ago. He now has sharp, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) substernal chest pain that is worse lying flat and eases when he leans forward. A pericardial friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) is heard at the left sternal border, and the electrocardiogram shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and ST depression in aVR. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Myocardial infarction is a common differential, but pericardial pain is pleuritic and positional unlike infarction, and widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression is the pericarditis pattern.
Pleuritis is a differential, but a pleural rub is heard only during inspiration, and widespread ST elevation with PR depression is the pattern of acute pericarditis.

Correct. Sharp pleuritic, positional pain after a viral illness, a friction rub and widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression (reciprocal changes in aVR) meet three of the four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis; two are enough.
Pulmonary embolism is a less common differential; positional pain eased by leaning forward, a friction rub and widespread ST elevation with PR depression point to pericarditis instead.

opts: Transcutaneous pacing pads pace a slow heart in an emergency. The wearable defibrillator vest is the worn device that shocks.

ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. There is a wearable (external) cardioverter defibrillator, worn as a vest, that detects fatal ventricular arrhythmias and delivers a shock.
A Holter monitor records the rhythm for a day or two but cannot shock. The wearable defibrillator vest detects and shocks fatal rhythms.

The ankle-brachial index is the initial test for peripheral artery disease in the legs. Carotid stenosis is first assessed with duplex ultrasonography.
Digital subtraction angiography is the invasive gold standard, not used for screening; it guides therapeutic interventions. The initial carotid test is duplex ultrasonography.

Stones and gout are unrelated to arterial bypass. He should hear about myocardial infarction, stroke, graft infection and peripheral embolization.
Hoarseness and dysphagia are compression symptoms of thoracic aortic aneurysms of the arch and descending aorta. Bypass risks are infarction, stroke, graft infection and embolization.

D.q: A 47-year-old man has new dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 30%. He reports fatigue, heat intolerance and weight loss, and the conjunctivae look pale. Which initial laboratory tests are most useful for finding a contributing cause?
opts: Pancreatic enzymes are not part of the dilated cardiomyopathy work-up. The listed tests are a blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel, liver function and thyroid function.
Blood cultures and a throat swab
Cultures do not appear in the dilated cardiomyopathy laboratory panel. The panel looks for anemia, electrolyte and renal problems, liver disease and thyroid dysfunction.
Neither test is part of the listed work-up. Anemia is checked with a blood count and thyroid dysfunction with thyroid function tests, alongside metabolic and liver panels.
Thyroid function and a blood count

Correct. The initial laboratory work-up for dilated cardiomyopathy includes a complete blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel, liver function and thyroid function. His symptoms point to thyroid disease and anemia.

D.q: A 41-year-old woman is being treated for acute pericarditis with an anti-inflammatory and colchicine. She asks whether she may take brisk walks while recovering. Which heart rate ceiling should guide her activity?
opts: A ceiling of 60 would demand bradycardia and is not the target. The limit is a maximal heart rate under 100.
Correct. During the restriction, strenuous activity is avoided and the maximal heart rate is kept under 100 beats per minute, for at least 1 month and until symptoms and C-reactive protein normalize.
One hundred fifty permits vigorous exercise, which the restriction forbids. The ceiling is under 100 beats per minute.
No limit if she feels well
Feeling well is not the guide; the heart rate stays under 100 until the inflammation and symptoms resolve.

D.q: A 33-year-old man has had a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 for an hour. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/80. A properly performed vagal maneuver has not converted it. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; it has no role in ending a fast reentrant rhythm.
Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia; he is alert with a normal blood pressure, so adenosine comes next.

Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver and then adenosine, which may be given twice; it may convert the rhythm or at least slow it so any P waves can be seen.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway, an irregular wide rhythm; his is regular and narrow.

D.q: Which bacterial cause of pericarditis is linked to rheumatic pancarditis?
opts: Histoplasma is a fungal cause of pericarditis. Rheumatic pancarditis follows streptococcal infection.
Correct. Among the bacterial causes, Streptococcus is tied to rheumatic pancarditis; the others listed are Staphylococcus, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Mycoplasma is listed among bacterial causes of pericarditis but has no link to rheumatic fever; Streptococcus causes rheumatic pancarditis.
Staphylococcus is a bacterial cause of purulent pericarditis but is not the organism of rheumatic pancarditis, which is Streptococcus.

D.q: Andexanet alfa is the reversal agent for which pair of anticoagulants?
opts: Heparins are reversed by protamine sulfate. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab and warfarin by prothrombin complex concentrate. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Neither is reversed by andexanet alfa. It reverses the direct factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Correct. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban, the direct factor Xa inhibitors, and its use is off-label for edoxaban as well.

opts: Correct. Catheter ablation is used if premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; premature beats triggering fibrillation are targeted by ablation.
Myectomy treats obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it has no role in premature atrial beats.
Carotid surgery treats carotid artery stenosis; premature atrial beats that trigger fibrillation are ablated.

D.q: A 66-year-old woman has a large arteriovenous fistula of the thigh and a positive Nicoladoni-Branham sign (slowing of the heart rate when the fistula is compressed). Her resting pulse is 88 beats per minute. Which action should the examiner avoid?
opts: Listening over it for a bruit
Auscultation is part of the standard examination and carries no risk to the heart rate. Diagnosis of a fistula is made on physical examination, including the bruit.
Feeling for a thrill over it
Light palpation for a thrill does not compress the fistula and is safe. Palpation is a core part of the examination that establishes the diagnosis.
Distal pulses should be checked to look for evidence of ischemia. This routine assessment does not compress a large fistula and does not trigger a reflex slowing of the heart.
Correct. Compressing a large fistula reflexly slows the heart rate, so sustained manual compression risks a significant fall in pulse and should be avoided during the examination.

D.q: A 79-year-old man with cardiomyopathy has become lightheaded on standing since his medications were increased at his last visit. He is frail and has lost weight. Which parts of his drug therapy call for particular caution at his age?
opts: Sodium restriction is a lifestyle measure, not a drug, and it is part of adult cardiomyopathy care. The medications singled out for caution in the elderly are diuretics and vasodilators.

Correct. Age-specific strategies for elderly patients with cardiomyopathy call for cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators, with therapy tailored to comorbidity and frailty and a focus on symptom control.
Device follow-up is not the concern here. His lightheadedness after medication changes fits the elderly caution about diuretics and vasodilators.
Home-based rehabilitation is recommended for elderly or mobility-limited patients and is not a drug. Caution in the elderly applies to diuretics and vasodilators.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
D.q: A 77-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted in respiratory failure. Her rhythm is irregular at 125, with a P wave before every narrow QRS in at least three different shapes. Which is the mainstay of management for this rhythm?
opts: Anticoagulation addresses stroke risk in atrial fibrillation and flutter; multifocal atrial tachycardia has discrete P waves and is managed by treating its cause.
Synchronized cardioversion is for an unstable tachycardia such as unstable atrial fibrillation; multifocal atrial tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying condition.
Catheter ablation is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia, from a single focus; multifocal atrial tachycardia comes from several foci driven by the illness.

Correct. An irregular, narrow-complex tachycardia with at least three P-wave shapes is multifocal atrial tachycardia, usually from acutely ill severe lung disease or heart failure; management is to treat the underlying condition.

D.q: Pericarditis symptoms that persist beyond 4 to 6 weeks, up to 3 months, without a sustained remission define which form?
opts: Correct. Incessant pericarditis is when symptoms persist for more than 4 to 6 weeks and up to 3 months without a sustained remission; past 3 months the label becomes chronic.
Constrictive pericarditis is a structural diagnosis, fibrous scarring with loss of pericardial elasticity, not a time label. The persistent course described is incessant pericarditis.
Chronic pericarditis is the label once symptoms persist for more than 3 months. Persistence from 4 to 6 weeks up to 3 months is called incessant.
Recurrent pericarditis needs a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before symptoms return. Unbroken persistence up to 3 months is incessant pericarditis instead.

D.q: A 17-year-old who injects drugs has fever, rigors and a tricuspid valve vegetation. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Coagulase-negative staphylococci follow prosthetic material or recent surgery; injection drug use brings Staphylococcus aureus.
Correct. Adolescents increasingly resemble adults, including injection drug use-associated Staphylococcus aureus disease, which dominates tricuspid infection.
Viridans streptococci lead in younger children with congenital heart disease; injection drug use points to Staphylococcus aureus.
Candida is tied to neonatal catheters and hyperalimentation, not adolescent injection drug use.

D.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
D.q: A 70-year-old man has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Two separate blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus, a transesophageal echocardiogram shows no vegetation, and he has no predisposing heart condition, no drug use and no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: A normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis, and the two positive cultures still meet a major criterion.
Two separate cultures of Staphylococcus aureus meet the major blood culture criterion, and his fever is a minor criterion.
Definite would need a second major criterion, three minor criteria with the one major, or five minor. He has one major and one minor.
Correct. He has one major criterion (a typical organism, Staphylococcus aureus, in two separate cultures) and one minor criterion (fever), which makes endocarditis possible.

D.q: Which pseudoaneurysms may be managed by watching and waiting?
opts: Large pseudoaneurysms are unlikely to seal on their own. Watch and wait is for those under 2 cm.
The typical pseudoaneurysm is femoral, not aortic. Watch and wait is for any under 2 cm.
Correct. A pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm in diameter may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression, so watch and wait; otherwise an ultrasound-guided thrombin injection seals the leak.
Symptomatic compression argues for treatment. Watch and wait suits pseudoaneurysms under 2 cm.

opts: Both the condition and the procedure qualify: high-risk heart disease plus incision of respiratory mucosa.
Prophylaxis is given before the procedure so the drug is circulating when bacteremia occurs.

Correct. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is a high-risk pediatric condition, and tonsillectomy is an invasive respiratory procedure with mucosal incision, so prophylaxis is given beforehand.
Surgery need not be canceled; a single prophylactic dose before the tonsillectomy is the recommended approach.

E.q: A 27-year-old woman has had 20 minutes of sudden palpitations. Her heart rate is 188, blood pressure 122/76, and she is alert with no chest pain or breathlessness. The electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Intravenous procainamide is used for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not as a first step; a stable narrow complex tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.
Correct. A stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia above 160 with hidden P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and the first-line treatment when stable is a vagal maneuver, then adenosine.
Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.
Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver fails.

E.q: A 17-year-old soccer player had an episode of racing heartbeat that stopped on its own. His resting tracing, taken in sinus rhythm, is shown. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Progressively longer PR, then a dropped beat
PR lengthening until a QRS drops is Mobitz type I block; here every P wave is followed by a QRS, and the striking feature is the slurred start of each QRS.
Long PR with every P wave conducted
A PR interval over 0.20 seconds with every P wave conducted is first-degree atrioventricular block; on this tracing the P wave runs almost straight into the QRS, so the PR is short.
Irregular rhythm with no P waves
No P waves and an irregular rhythm describe atrial fibrillation; this tracing is in sinus rhythm, with a P wave before every QRS.
ruled out by a stated finding
Short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke

Correct. A short PR interval with a slurred upstroke of the QRS (the delta wave) in sinus rhythm is pre-excitation, consistent with an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
E.alt: Close-up rhythm strip of three beats, each with a small P wave running into a QRS whose upstroke is gradual before the main spike

E.q: A 68-year-old man is brought in confused, with a blood pressure of 76/40. The monitor shows a slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is a timed shock for an unstable tachycardia with a pulse; unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine first.

Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia is treated first with atropine; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent one.
A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acutely unstable patient first gets atropine, then temporary pacing.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.

E.q: A 59-year-old man with three coronary stents and no valve disease needs a tooth extracted. He asks whether he needs antibiotics before the procedure. Which advice is most accurate?
opts: Coronary stents are not a high-risk condition, so amoxicillin prophylaxis is not indicated.
Stents are not removed, and they do not create a need for endocarditis prophylaxis.

Correct. Prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk conditions (prosthetic valves or valve-repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation); coronary stents are not among them.
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of Clostridioides difficile risk, and he does not need prophylaxis at all.

E.q: Which electrolyte disturbances are named triggers of premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Low calcium and high sodium are not the named triggers. The list is hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia.
Correct. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, along with hypercalcemia, are the electrolyte imbalances named as causes of premature ventricular contractions.
Phosphate and chloride are not named. The electrolyte triggers listed are hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia.
Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia are not the named triggers. Low potassium, low magnesium and high calcium are listed.

E.q: A 58-year-old man with suspected tamponade has distended jugular veins and a blood pressure of 88/60. He has leg edema, and drainage is being arranged. Which drug class should be avoided?
opts: Antibiotics are not indicated for every tamponade, but they are not the harmful class here; diuretics are.
Intravenous fluids are the temporizing support in tamponade, raising preload until pericardiocentesis; they are not avoided.
Local anesthesia is used for the pericardiocentesis itself and is not a concern here.
Correct. Fluid resuscitation is given in tamponade to increase preload and prevent right ventricular collapse, so diuretics, which reduce preload, should be avoided before drainage.

E.q: A 64-year-old woman has two weeks of exertional breathlessness and chest pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block; a tracing from last year was normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. A new left bundle branch block should always be considered a sign of pathology, so it is worked up for the underlying cardiac disease or injury rather than dismissed.
Cardioversion terminates tachycardias; a conduction block with a normal rate is not shocked. The new block needs a workup.
Some new right bundle branch blocks occur without heart disease, but a new left bundle branch block is a sign of pathology that needs evaluation.
Left bundle branch block is usually not paced unless it is symptomatic with reduced ejection fraction, which calls for a biventricular device after evaluation.
