Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
E.q: A 64-year-old woman must stay in bed for several days after major abdominal surgery. Her team wants a preventive measure aimed at the venous stasis component of the Virchow triad. Which measure is most appropriate?
opts: Warm compresses are a comfort measure for superficial phlebitis and do nothing to keep deep venous blood moving. Intermittent pneumatic compression mimics the muscle pump and counters stasis.

An inferior vena cava filter catches clots after they form and is reserved for acute proximal deep vein thrombosis when anticoagulation is contraindicated. It is not a routine preventive measure for stasis after surgery.

Thrombolysis breaks down an existing clot in selected patients with a large proximal deep vein thrombosis or stable pulmonary embolism. It treats established clots and carries bleeding risk, so it is not prevention.

Correct. Intermittent pneumatic compression, sequential devices that squeeze the legs in turn, imitates the calf muscle pump and keeps blood moving, countering stasis. It is used especially when a patient is immobilized after surgery or hospitalized for long.

opts: Correct. Sawtooth waves conducted 2:1 make atrial flutter; when hemodynamically stable it is treated with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker for rate control, though control is harder to reach than in atrial fibrillation.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway; stable atrial flutter is treated with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter; he is alert with a normal blood pressure, so rate control comes first.
A permanent pacemaker treats symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; a fast, stable atrial flutter needs rate control and later ablation.

E.q: In unstable Mobitz type II block, when medications are not used or do not work, which is the emergent measure?
opts: Correct. Transcutaneous pacing, with pads on the chest, is the emergent measure for unstable Mobitz type II block; it bridges the patient to a permanent pacemaker.
Vagal maneuvers slow atrioventricular conduction and would worsen a block. The emergent measure is transcutaneous pacing.
Synchronized cardioversion treats unstable tachycardias with a pulse. A failing conduction system with a slow rate needs pacing, not a shock.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Unstable Mobitz type II block is paced transcutaneously.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
E.q: A 66-year-old man has right-sided heart failure with a raised jugular venous pressure and ascites. Echocardiogram shows abnormal diastolic filling, normal-sized ventricles and big atria, but the team cannot tell restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis. Which test is used to differentiate them?
opts: Echocardiography alone is not definitive for this distinction, so repeating it adds little. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can show the pericardial thickening that points to constriction.

Gram-negative bacilli are uncommon causes of endocarditis. Late prosthetic valve infection is viridans streptococcal.
Candida causes fungal endocarditis, mostly with immunocompromise or central lines; the late prosthetic valve organism is viridans streptococci.
Staphylococcus epidermidis is the classic early prosthetic valve organism; 4 years out, viridans streptococci are expected.

ruled out by a stated finding

E.alt: Three rows of a rhythm strip: bursts of rapid narrow complexes that stop abruptly, then long flat pauses before slower beats resume

A cavity outside the vessel wall

An intimal tear with a false lumen

Correct. Premature atrial contractions in a normal heart with excess alcohol, stress or caffeine are benign: counsel avoidance of precipitants and reassure about the benign nature of the rhythm.
Anticoagulation is for atrial fibrillation and flutter; isolated premature atrial beats need none.

E.q: A 70-year-old man has claudication after half a block despite six months of supervised exercise, smoking cessation and cilostazol, and can no longer work. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Revascularization is recommended for claudication with severe functional disability and an inadequate response to exercise or drug therapy, by endovascular angioplasty with or without stenting, atherectomy, or bypass.
Amputation is a last resort for nonviable limbs or failed revascularization. Disabling claudication without tissue loss first goes to revascularization.
Intravenous heparin is for acute limb ischemia, the sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery. Chronic disabling claudication after failed therapy calls for revascularization.
He has already had an adequate supervised trial and remains severely disabled. The recommended escalation after failed exercise and drugs is revascularization.

E.q: A 45-year-old woman who drinks four cups of coffee a day feels occasional skipped beats. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 78, interrupted by an early beat with an abnormally shaped P wave followed by a narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A premature ventricular contraction is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave in front; this early beat is narrow and has its own P wave.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. An early beat with its own abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS is a premature atrial contraction, which can occur in normal hearts with stress, caffeine or excess alcohol.
A premature junctional contraction is early and narrow but has an inverted P wave, a hidden P wave or a P wave after the QRS, not an abnormal upright P before it.
Mobitz type I lengthens the PR until a QRS drops, so it produces a missing beat, not an early beat with an abnormal P wave.

E.q: A 58-year-old man on telemetry develops a run of identical wide QRS complexes at 180 per minute. Within 18 seconds his blood pressure falls to 70/40 and he loses consciousness, and the team shocks him back to sinus rhythm. How should this episode be classified?
opts: Bigeminy alternates normal and ectopic beats. A continuous run of wide complexes is ventricular tachycardia.
Under 30 seconds counts as non-sustained only when the patient stays stable. A run that causes hemodynamic collapse in under 30 seconds, as his did, is sustained.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia counts as sustained if it lasts 30 seconds or more or causes hemodynamic collapse in under 30 seconds; his hypotension makes an 18-second run sustained.
Fibrillation is disorganized activity with no pulse. Identical wide complexes at a regular rate are ventricular tachycardia.

E.q: A 52-year-old man starts outpatient treatment for deep vein thrombosis with low molecular weight heparin injections overlapped with warfarin. The injections continue for at least five days and until his international normalized ratio is above which value?
opts: An international normalized ratio just above 1 is barely different from normal, so warfarin has not yet taken effect. The overlap continues until the value is above 2.

Correct. Parenteral therapy overlaps with warfarin for at least five days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2, when warfarin has reached its therapeutic effect and the heparin can stop.
The overlap ends once the international normalized ratio is above 2, the therapeutic threshold for this indication. Waiting for a value above 3 would prolong the injections without benefit.
An international normalized ratio above 4 is over-anticoagulated and raises the bleeding risk. The heparin overlap stops once warfarin is therapeutic, at a value above 2.

E.q: A 67-year-old former smoker with weight loss has a large pericardial effusion. Lung cancer is suspected, and pericardiocentesis is performed. Which study of the pericardial fluid best addresses this suspicion?
opts: Gram stain looks for bacteria in purulent pericarditis, not for cancer cells. Cytology does.
Cell count and differential are rarely helpful in establishing the diagnosis. Cytology looks for malignant cells.
Correct. Pericardial fluid is sent for cell count, Gram stain, cultures, acid-fast studies and cytology, and cytology is the study that identifies malignant cells.
Fungal culture detects fungal infection, not malignancy. Cytology addresses suspected lung cancer.

E.q: A 66-year-old man with a known ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm develops a new diastolic murmur, exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. Which complication does the aneurysm's location explain?
opts: Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, with hoarseness, comes from an arch aneurysm. The ascending aorta causes aortic regurgitation and heart failure.
Correct. An ascending thoracic aneurysm can cause aortic regurgitation and heart failure, which explains the new diastolic murmur, breathlessness and edema.
Tracheal compression with stridor and wheeze comes from a descending aneurysm. The ascending location explains aortic regurgitation.
Esophageal compression with dysphagia is a descending aneurysm effect. An ascending aneurysm produces aortic regurgitation and heart failure.

E.q: What is the etiology of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Plaque rupture is absent by definition; angiographic coronary disease is not found. The etiology is unknown.
Viral infection is the presumed commonest cause of myocarditis. Stress cardiomyopathy has an unknown etiology.
Amyloid infiltration causes restrictive cardiomyopathy. The etiology of stress cardiomyopathy is unknown.
Correct. The etiology of stress cardiomyopathy is unknown; what is known is that a significant emotional or physical stressor precedes it.

E.q: A 72-year-old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.2 cm, unchanged from last year. Which follow-up is most appropriate?
opts: Emergency surgery is for a ruptured aneurysm with pain, a pulsatile mass and hypotension. An asymptomatic, stable 4.2 cm aneurysm is surveyed every six to 12 months.
Correct. Surveillance frequency depends on size: an aneurysm of 4.0 to 5.4 cm is imaged with ultrasound or computed tomography every six to 12 months.
At 4.2 cm and not growing, he is below every repair threshold (5.0 cm women, over 5.5 cm men, or 0.5 cm growth in six months). Surveillance continues.
Three-yearly ultrasound is for aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm. At 4.2 cm the interval shortens to every six to 12 months.

E.q: A 66-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy develops a new holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex that radiates to the left axilla. Her ventricle has continued to enlarge on serial echocardiograms. Which complication best accounts for the new murmur?
opts: Correct. As the ventricle dilates, the valve apparatus is distorted, and mitral regurgitation (which appears earlier) and tricuspid regurgitation commonly develop. The mitral murmur is holosystolic at the apex, radiating to the axilla.
Outflow obstruction from a thick septum
Septal outflow obstruction belongs to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and gives a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border that does not radiate to the axilla.
Pericardial thickening marks constrictive pericarditis, the differential of restrictive cardiomyopathy. It does not create a holosystolic apical murmur.
Tricuspid regurgitation is heard at the lower left sternal border and radiates along the sternum, not to the axilla. An apical murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
E.q: A 15-year-old boy is seen for a sports physical. He has no symptoms, but his father was recently diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Which strategy for this adolescent is most appropriate?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden death in preadolescents and adolescents, so evaluation should not wait. Genetic screening is the adolescent strategy.
An endomyocardial biopsy at this visit
Biopsy has no role in screening relatives. The adolescent strategy for a family history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is genetic screening.

Correct. Age-specific strategies for adolescents include genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and disease detected in a family member is a common reason evaluation begins. One affected parent is enough to pass it on.
A routine chest radiograph each year
The chest radiograph may be normal in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and is not a screening tool. Adolescents with an affected parent get genetic screening.

E.q: A 57-year-old man with superficial thrombophlebitis of the calf was started on compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug. At his recheck nine days later, the tender cord has lengthened and the redness has spread up the leg. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Progression despite treatment means the plan is not working and the extent of clot is unknown. Imaging with duplex ultrasound is needed before simply continuing the same care.
Place an inferior vena cava filter

Filters are limited to acute proximal lower extremity deep vein thrombosis with active bleeding or another contraindication to anticoagulation. Worsening superficial disease is first reimaged with duplex ultrasound.
The first recheck at 7 to 10 days already showed progression. Delaying further risks missed extension, and the response to worsening is a repeat duplex ultrasound.

Correct. Persistence or worsening of signs and symptoms at the 7 to 10 day recheck calls for a repeat duplex ultrasound to look for extension of the clot, since the superficial clot may now need different therapy.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: A 66-year-old man with subacute endocarditis has a fundoscopic examination that shows Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages). What process causes these spots?
opts: Hypertension causes its own retinopathy. Roth spots reflect vasculitis of small retinal arteries in endocarditis.
Raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc; it does not make white-centered hemorrhages.
Trauma and detachment are not the mechanism. Roth spots come from vasculitis of the small retinal arteries.
Correct. Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages from vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina, grouped with the immunologic phenomena in the Duke criteria.

E.q: A 35-year-old woman has abrupt-onset palpitations. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 170, with one P wave of the same abnormal shape before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has a uniform, normal P wave and runs from 100 to 160; her P waves are abnormal in shape and the rate is 170.
ruled out by a stated finding
Nodal reentrant tachycardia hides its P waves, a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node; she has a visible abnormal P wave before every QRS.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in the same lead; her rhythm is regular with one P-wave shape.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with one consistently abnormal P wave before each QRS comes from a single ectopic focus in the atria outside the sinus node: focal atrial tachycardia, which typically begins abruptly.

E.q: An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 appears in someone with a known accessory pathway. Which intravenous drug is used?
opts: Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia approaching 300 with an accessory pathway is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, treated with intravenous procainamide, never adenosine.
Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.
Adenosine must never be used here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.
Atropine speeds conduction and is used for unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster, not slower.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
E.q: In sinus arrhythmia, how does the heart rate change with breathing?
opts: A changing P-wave shape with an irregular rate suggests multifocal atrial tachycardia. Sinus arrhythmia keeps uniform P waves while the rate follows breathing.
Faster in both phases of the breath
The rate does not rise throughout the breath; it rises with inspiration and slows with expiration, which is what makes the rhythm irregular with a pattern.
Slower on inspiration, faster on expiration
This reverses the pattern. In sinus arrhythmia the sinus rate rises during inspiration and falls during expiration.
Faster on inspiration, slower on expiration
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is irregular with a pattern: the sinus rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration, while every beat keeps a normal P wave and narrow QRS.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
E.q: Which complete blood count pattern is expected in infective endocarditis?
opts: Eosinophilia and macrocytosis are not the pattern. Leukocytosis and normocytic anemia of chronic disease are.
Correct. The complete blood count with differential shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume (normocytic).
A low white count with small red cells is not the expected pattern. Expect leukocytosis and normocytic anemia of chronic disease.
Polycythemia is not expected. Infection raises the white count, and chronic inflammation causes a normocytic anemia.

E.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
E.q: A 58-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve has a fever of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F) and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). No blood cultures or echocardiogram have been done yet. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Correct. He has three minor criteria: a predisposing heart condition (prosthetic valve), fever, and a vascular phenomenon (conjunctival hemorrhages). Three minor criteria make endocarditis possible.
Fever, the prosthetic valve and the conjunctival hemorrhages are each a minor criterion: three in all.
Definite needs two major, one major and three minor, or five minor criteria. Three minor criteria only reach possible.
Nothing here excludes endocarditis: a prosthetic valve, fever and conjunctival hemorrhages are three minor criteria, which make it possible.

E.q: A 68-year-old man has a 3.1 cm femoral pseudoaneurysm that has persisted since his catheterization. Which treatment seals the leak?
opts: Correct. Treatment of a pseudoaneurysm that does not regress is ultrasound-guided injection of thrombin, which promotes clotting and seals the leak.
Heparin prevents the clotting that seals the cavity. The leak is sealed by ultrasound-guided thrombin injection.
Thrombolysis is for acute arterial thrombus under 14 days. A pseudoaneurysm is sealed by promoting clot, with ultrasound-guided thrombin.
Watchful waiting is for pseudoaneurysms under 2 cm, which may thrombose on their own. A persistent 3.1 cm cavity needs thrombin injection.

E.q: Carotid angioplasty with stenting is chosen for which patients?
opts: Correct. Carotid stenting, most commonly through the common femoral artery, is less invasive and allows intervention in poor surgical candidates; endarterectomy remains the gold standard.
Stenosis under 50% is managed medically. Stenting is for patients who need intervention but are poor surgical candidates.
Most asymptomatic patients are managed medically. Stenting is chosen for poor surgical candidates who meet surgical thresholds.
Limited life expectancy argues against intervention in asymptomatic disease. Stenting is for poor surgical candidates.

E.q: A 25-year-old woman has newly diagnosed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a septum of 2.2 cm and occasional palpitations. Her cardiologist wants to judge her risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Which test assesses that risk?
opts: Catheterization is not required for diagnosis and is kept for when a pacemaker or surgery is planned. Arrhythmia risk is assessed with ambulatory monitoring.
Genetic testing is available but does not influence treatment, and it does not grade her arrhythmia risk. Ambulatory rhythm monitoring does.
Correct. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours should be performed in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to assess the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.
The chest radiograph may be normal in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and says nothing about arrhythmia. Ambulatory monitoring for 24 to 48 hours assesses that risk.

E.q: A 29-year-old woman has acute pericarditis with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) and widespread ST elevation. Her clinician wants laboratory values that confirm inflammation and can guide the length of therapy. Which pair of tests is most appropriate?
opts: Cultures are for suspected bacterial disease. Routine monitoring uses sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.
Pancreatic and liver enzymes do not gauge pericardial inflammation. Sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein do.

Correct. The initial workup includes complete blood count, troponins, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein; the C-reactive protein is checked at presentation and weekly to guide tapering.
D-dimer is not part of this workup and the natriuretic peptide is used in constriction. Inflammation is measured with sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.

E.q: A 70-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure has atrial flutter (sawtooth flutter waves) with a ventricular rate of 140. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 and no chest pain. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; she is stable, so rate control comes first.
A beta or calcium channel blocker
Correct. Hemodynamically stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; rate control is the first goal, though harder to achieve than in fibrillation.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; flutter at 140 needs rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Adenosine is used for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: A 55-year-old man has a preoperative electrocardiogram and no symptoms. The rhythm is sinus at 72, the QRS lasts 0.16 seconds, V1 to V3 show an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection, bunny ears), and there is a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Left bundle branch block widens the QRS with a dominant S wave (rS) in V1 and monophasic R waves in the lateral leads; an rsR' in V1 to V3 is right-sided.

Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with an rsR' pattern (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL is right bundle branch block; it is usually asymptomatic and is not always pathologic when new.
Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave); a second upward deflection in V1 to V3 is a right bundle branch block.
Ventricular tachycardia is a wide rhythm at 100 to 250 with no P waves tied to the QRS; he is in sinus rhythm at 72.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: A 62-year-old man was shocked out of unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia 3 days ago and is now stable in sinus rhythm. Which is the most appropriate long-term measure to prevent sudden cardiac death?
opts: Ablating an accessory pathway is first-line long-term treatment for Wolff-Parkinson-White; survivors of life-threatening ventricular tachycardia need an implantable defibrillator.

Correct. Once stabilized, most patients who had life-threatening ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation need an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death; it senses fatal arrhythmias and delivers a shock.
A pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or calcium channel blocker is an option for nodal reentrant tachycardia; after life-threatening ventricular tachycardia he needs a defibrillator.
A permanent pacemaker treats symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; it cannot shock a recurrence of ventricular tachycardia, which needs a defibrillator.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
E.q: A 30-year-old marathon runner has no symptoms. A lead II tracing taken at rest is shown; the rate is 48. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus bradycardia, also common in athletes, has an upright P wave before every QRS; this tracing shows no P wave before any of the complexes.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; these complexes are evenly spaced, slow and regular, with no fibrillating baseline.
Third-degree block shows P waves marching at their own rate, unrelated to a slow escape rhythm; this tracing has no P waves to march.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 40 to 60 with no P waves visible (hidden in the QRS) is a junctional rhythm, which can be seen in healthy, well-conditioned athletes with increased vagal tone.
E.alt: Lead II rhythm strip of five narrow complexes at a slow, regular rate, each followed by a T wave, with no P wave visible before any complex

E.q: After a first recurrence of pericarditis, colchicine is typically continued for how long?
opts: Two weeks is far too short for colchicine after a recurrence; the course is 6 months or more.
About 3 months is the colchicine course for a first episode. After a recurrence, colchicine continues for 6 months or more.
Correct. A first recurrence is treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug until pain resolves and inflammatory markers normalize, plus colchicine for 6 months or more.
Colchicine is not given for life. After a first recurrence it is continued for 6 months or more.

E.q: A 74-year-old woman with known aortic atherosclerosis has sudden pain and tenderness of two toes, which have turned blue. Which pulse finding is expected on examination?
opts: A pulse with a double systolic peak
A double-peaked pulse is not a feature of limb emboli. With atheroembolism the expected finding is that distal pulses usually remain palpable.
Absent or diminished femoral pulses suggest aortoiliac disease, as in Leriche syndrome. Blue toes from atheroemboli usually come with palpable distal pulses.
Correct. Atheroembolic debris tends to lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, so distal pulses usually remain palpable, unlike acute limb ischemia.
Pulses absent below the femoral artery
Absent pulses distal to an occlusion are the finding of acute limb ischemia from a thromboembolus. Small-vessel atheroemboli usually leave distal pulses palpable.

E.q: A 72-year-old man has months of progressive breathlessness, abdominal swelling and bilateral pedal edema. He prefers to sit upright. Jugular venous pressure is raised and he has a Kussmaul sign (jugular venous pressure rises with inspiration), hepatomegaly and ascites. His electrocardiogram shows low voltage (small complexes) in all leads, and echocardiogram shows normal-sized ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Stiff ventricles with a near-normal cavity, preserved ejection fraction and big atria, presenting late with right-sided failure, are restrictive cardiomyopathy; low voltage points to amyloidosis, the most common cause in the United States.
Dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with a reduced ejection fraction. Normal-sized ventricles with a preserved fraction and big atria are restrictive.
Stress cardiomyopathy is a sudden, transient apical weakness after a stressor. Months of right-sided congestion with stiff ventricles and big atria is restrictive disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows asymmetric septal thickening with an outflow murmur and prominent Q waves rather than low voltage. Right-sided congestion with big atria fits restrictive disease.

E.q: A 26-year-old man with suspected viral myocarditis has an elevated troponin and normal coronary arteries. His cardiologist wants to see how much of the heart muscle is inflamed without an invasive procedure. Which test shows the extent of inflammation?
opts: Correct. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging is part of the myocarditis work-up because the gadolinium improves visibility of the inflammation and shows its extent.
Right heart catheterization with pressure tracings
Pressure tracings help evaluate restrictive physiology. Inflammation is shown noninvasively by gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging.
Exercise echocardiography assesses functional capacity, ischemia and obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It does not show the extent of inflammation.
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours
Ambulatory monitoring detects arrhythmias and grades sudden death risk, most notably in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It cannot show inflamed heart muscle.

E.q: A 63-year-old woman is diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis. She had mantle-field radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 25 years ago and is otherwise well. Which feature of her history most worsens her long-term prognosis?
opts: The lymphoma itself is cured; it is the radiation used to treat it that predicts the worst survival.
Sex is not named as a determinant of survival. Prior ionizing radiation carries the worst prognosis.
Comorbidities worsen the outlook, so their absence helps. Her prior radiation is what worsens it.
Correct. Etiology is an important determinant of survival in constrictive pericarditis, and prior ionizing radiation is associated with the worst survival rates.

E.q: A 45-year-old man who grew up in rural Bolivia has months of fatigue and exertional breathlessness. His heart rate is 38 and the electrocardiogram shows P waves completely dissociated from slow, wide QRS complexes. Which infection is a named cause of his conduction disease?
opts: Tuberculosis is not on the list of causes of complete block. Chagas disease, endemic in Latin America, is.
Correct. Chagas disease is a named cause of complete heart block; it is a parasitic infection endemic in parts of Latin America such as rural Bolivia.
Lyme carditis is a named cause of block, but it follows a tick bite in endemic areas such as New England. His background points to Chagas disease.
Malaria is not a named cause of complete block. A man from rural Bolivia with complete block suggests Chagas disease.
